PRIVILEGE-Mr. DENIS

I rise to a question of privilege. Speaking in Committee of Supply, on the Estimates of Immigration, on April 26 last, I said that I was in favour of admitting into Canada the immigrants of Europe, the subjects of former enemy nations included, provided these immigrants be morally and physically fit, and of the desirable class that we want in this country. Incidentally, I also made reference to the question of unemployment.
Commenting upon my remarks, some newspapers in the province of Quebec said that I had expressed the view that I would not be adverse to the idea of bringing into this country immigrants who- would eventually take the jobs of our working men. I wish emphatically to protest, Sir, against any such interpretation being given to my remarks. By no means do I want foreigners to come to this country to the detriment of our honest working classes. What I said, and what I still maintain, is that this country is wide enough and has resources enough to allow hundreds of thousands of immigrants to come here without any detriment to any class of the population, but, on the contrary, to the mutual benefit of all classes.

speechtext: Hon. HUGH GUTHRIE (Acting Solicitor General) moved the second reading of Bill No. 130, to amend the Dominion Elections Act.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (leader of the Opposition) :
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I assume that the
statement which was made by the hon. Solicitor General in moving the first reading of this Bill is correct, namely, that it simply embodies the different recommendations which the Chief Electoral Officer presented to the Committee on Privileges and Elections and which were unanimously
MAY 9, lf>21
approved by that committee. As far as I can see in looking over the Bill, these recommendations appear to relate exclusively to matters of administration, and have nothing whatever to do with any question of principle involved in the Act. I would ask the minister if, when the Bill goes into committee, he will be prepared to consider other amendments than those which are embodied in the Bill. There are two or three features of the Dominion Elections Act which by-elections recently held disclose to be in the public interest. There is one clause in particular which has been strongly objected to by members on this side of the House, the clause relating to a class of voters who have to appear before a judge in order to get a voting certificate before they are allowed to vote. That is a clause that should come up for further consideration when the Bill is before the House. Will my hon. friend state whether he will be prepared to consider either amending the Bill in this and other respects at the present time, or referring certain amendments to the Committee on Privileges and Elections for their consideration at this present session?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Before the hon. minister rises to speak, I must remind the House that lie will be exercising his right to close the debate, and if any other hon. member desires to speak upon the second reading, he should do so now.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: The leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King), is correct in his statement that this Bill follows with precision the recommendations made by the Chief Electoral Officer to his Honour the Speaker, pursuant to the terms of the Dominion Elections Act, and the Bill as now presented embodies only amendments which were prepared by the' Chief Electoral Officer, considered by the Committee on Privileges and Elections, and unanimously agreed to and reported to this House. No other amendments are proposed by the Government. But I do not see that there can be any objection to considering other amendments when the Bill is in committee.

On section 3-revising officers:	.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
The former rule 11 was said to be cumbersome and difficult of interpretation. The object of this amendment is to clarify the rule as far as possible, and correct some apparent errors in it. The former rule did not provide for duties being performed by district judges in any province but the province of Quebec. Now we have district judges in the province of Ontario, and that fact was overlooked last session. In the northern portions of Ontario there are district judges.
*

There is a schedule of
fees for the payment of judges, but what about those persons whom they may appoint when they are unable to act? Is there any provision for the payment of a man whom the judge appoints, when he cannot attend to all the business, to act in place of himself?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
Paragraph (d) provides as follows:
The duties hereby imposed upon judges shall be deemed to have been imposed upon, and to have been performable by them since the thirtieth day of June, 1920, and any fees allowed to revising officers by any tariff of fees approved under section seventy-six of this Act shall be payable to judges who hereafter personally undertake the revision of lists of voters.
It is an addition to the judicial salary of course.

But a judge is authorized to appoint another man in his place under this Act. A judge who has two or three counties to look after, as is the case in our province, and can only attend to one county himself, has power to appoint somebody else in another county. There appears to be no provision for the payment of that man.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: I think that such substitute may exercise all powers and perform all duties. I would think one of his functions would be to receive the fees prescribed by this Act.
Why not make it perfectly clear by adding "that the fees shall be paid to the judge or any person appointed by him"?

Is it deemed expedient that judges should be paid for doing this work? We have recently increased the salaries of judges and therefore why have we to pay them extra. I object to the whole idea. I think a good salary should be given to a judge-I do not at all object to that-but he should not get extras in any shape or form for the performance of the duties which pertain to his office.

There is also this fact to be borne in mind: On Friday, I think it was, we had a little discussion in the House about judges who might be called upon to preside over inquiries or investigations, and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) refused to concur in an amendment made by the Senate debarring judges from accepting such positions. The right hon. gen-tlemati stated that last year, when the Judges' Act was amended, and salaries of the judges were increased, and so increased with the idea of debarring them in future from accepting any remuneration where they presided over inquiries or special investigations. The increased salaries granted to judges, therefore, debars them from accepting any other remuneration. In the case of this legislation they are carrying out the provisions of the Dominion Elections Act, and it seems to me they should not receive any special remuneration in the matter.

That may apply all
right to a judge, but the man whom the judge appoints gets no remuneration at all. Surely he should be paid for his work, but apparently no provision has been made for that.

I quite concur that we should make provision to pay a substitute. It would be all right to do that. I do not think the substitute, who possibly gets no other remuneration from the Government, should be debarred from payment; we cannot expect him to work for nothing. But surely we have a right to expect that every judge in the Dominion of Canada who is in receipt of a salary-and if the salary is not sufficiently generous I would make it so -should perform these duties without receiving any extra remuneration in any shape or form.
If they do not get the extra remuneration will they not appoint substitutes in most cases?
Well, let them do it.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
There is no tariff of fees applicable to judges at the present time, but I suppose there is power in the Act to fix such a tariff. Section 76 of the Act is the one which applies in regard to the fees and expenses of election ^officers. It provides as follows:
Upon the recommendation of the Chief Electoral Officer, the Governor in Council may make a tariff of fees, costs, allowances and expenses to be paid and allowed to returning officers and other persons employed at or with respect to elections under this Act, and may, from time to time, revise and amend such tariff.
The judges are not specifically mentioned. I suppose they would be included in the general language "returning officers and other persons." When a tariff of fees is fixed the provision is that it should be laid before the House of Commons within the first fifteen days after the next ensuing session. The amendment does propose specifically to include judges. I suppose they would have been included under the former tariff under the words "other persons" although they are not named there as they are in the present proposal. '

But will my hon.
friend himself not volunteer an amendment that this provision shall not now apply to the judges? There is a principle in this matter. We have been increasing the salaries of the judges on the ground that the dignity and responsibilities of their office require generous treatment. I agree with that, I do not quarrel with giving any judge a generous salary; but I do ask the minister not to introduce in this legislation any provision to pay extra remuneration to judges,-I think it is a very undignified way for judges to get their money.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: On principle I agree with my hon. friend, but I think there must have been a reason in the mind of the Chief Electoral Officer when this clause was worded as it is. However, I will ask the committee to allow the clause to stand until I have had an opportunity of consulting with him.

All right.
Section stands.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I mentioned a moment ago that a test has been made of certain features of 'this Act and that some recent experiences have proven the existence of certain limitations in the measure, and I asked the minister if he would consider submitting some representations to the Committee on Privileges and Elections for their consideration. I would like to read him, if I might, part of a communication which I have received from the Attorney General of Alberta in reference to the powers of the registrars and the manner in which this clause in the Act operated in the taking of the recent plebiscite in that province. The communication is dated November 20, 1920:
We had a sample of how it worked in connection with taking the plebiscite in Alberta. The following are a few of the worst features of it:
1.	Registration is not made by polling subdivisions, and the person registering does not know what polling subdivision he will be placed in, even if his name be placed on the list.
2.	There is no means provided for any record which would be a check upon a dishonest registrar ; the voter appearing before the registrar is not required to sign anything and does not receive any document whereby he could prove that he had personally appeared and registered. The result is, and it happened in the recent plebiscite, that a man may appear before the registrar and think he has done everything to get his name on the list, and discovers afterwards that the registrar denies having ever seen him.
Then the communication contains a rather appropriate suggestion with reference to the practice followed in British Columbia regarding registration, which might be deserving of consideration:
British Columbia has the only fair registration system, and in that province all persons applying for registration sign an application. This application is placed on file by the registrar and the original is given to the deputy returning officer before polling day and is by him taken to the poll. When a voter comes to vote he is required to sign his name before he gets his ballot, and comparison can be made between " his signature and the original signature of the party who registered. This is not only a valuable
check against impersonation, but is some guarantee that the party actually appeared and made application to be placed upon the list.
I think the minister will see that these suggestions have considerable force, and while I am not prepared and would not like to take up the time of the committee in moving any formal amendment at the present time, I should like to suggest to my hon. friend that he consider whether these suggestions might not properly be referred to the committee on Privileges and Elections, with a view of having the Act amended in a manner that will make the registration more effective and less liable to be misinterpreted one way or the other.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
I have had a number
of discussions with the Chief Electoral Officer with regard to the manner in which the Election Act has worked in the various constituencies where it has been on trial, and from all I can gather from him it has worked exceptionally well and few, if any complaints have been received. It is the privilege and duty of successful and unsuccessful candidates after a by-election to make reports under the law of any defects or unsatisfactory conditions in the working of the Act. The suggestions are all brought to this House in the report of the Chief Electoral Officer. Any suggestions so far received are of very minor importance, in fact we have heard scarcely anything but commendation of the working of the Act. After discussing all the suggestions with the Chief Electoral Officer, he thinks that we have hardly had sufficient experience under the Act yet to see just where it can or can not be materially improved. I am satisfied that it has given pretty general satisfaction so far. One great objection to it, no doubt, in the future is going to be the fact that it will be a fairly expensive Act to administer. But, as to giving a complete record of persons entitled to vote which is up to date in every respect, I think it is a decided advance on any other Act we have ever had on the statute book.
I had an opportunity of discussing with the premier of British Columbia a few days ago the method adopted for indenti-fication of voters in his province, and he told me that the system was particularly necessary there because they had what was known as a "shifting vote" in almost eyery constituency, which in many instances would run to forty, fifty and sixty per cent of the total population. He said that under their system special steps had to be taken towards better indentification than was

probably necessary in the other provinces. I think that is a very good system, but it would be fairly cumbersome and slow and would add still further expense to the working out of this Act. It might be well that these suggestions should be considered at some future time, but I do not think at present they are of sufficient importance, nor have we sufficient information in regard to them, to delay the present Bill.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: These suggestions come from the Attorney General of Alberta, and he being the legal member of his government is probably the person best qualified to express an opinion on its behalf. I think representations coming from such a quarter in regard to actual experience under a plebiscite which of course relates to the working of the Act as a whole in that province, are of a character that the Government cannot regard too carefully. I hope my hon. friend will consider further the suggestion I have made of referring these with other possible suggestions to the committee on Privileges and Elections, and thereby perhaps avoid the necessity of any formal amendment in the House.

On section 5-copy of certified list for returning officer:

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
The section as at
present framed reads as follows:
Every registrar, having revised and corrected such retained copy of the voters' list compiled by him shall write at the foot of such copy and close to the last name thereon, on the ninth day before the polling day, a certificate in the form of the certificate contained in said Form No. 11 to this Act. He shall also on the same day deliver or mail by registered letter to the returning officer a copy of the list so certified-
Then follow these words, which should not be in the section at all:
-and the returning officer shall forthwith transmit the same to the Chief Electoral Officer.
Their retention would deprive the returning officer of his only copy of the list. Section agreed to.
On section 6-when new lists unnecessary :

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: What is that addition?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
Subsection 1 of section 32 at present reads:
Except as provided in tnis section, it shall not be necessary to prepare new lists of voters for the purposes of any election to be held in any electoral district when there has been in that electoral district a previous election for 
which the lists of voters prepared are of record in the office of the Electoral Officer and there is an interval of less than two years between the dates of the writs for the two elections.
The proposed amendment is in the first line, and is made by inserting after the word "except" the following words: "at a general election and". The section will then read:
Except at a general election and as provided in this section,-
And so on.

Section agreed to.
On section 7-indexed copies of Act or excerpts therefrom for election officers:

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: That, I think, Mr. Chairman, is a great improvement. The present law is that a copy of the Act shall be given to these officials and they shall be allowed to study and interpret it for themselves. Under this proposal the Chief Electoral Officer shall get up in concise form the main and important provisions of the Act in a way that will be easily intelligible to the ordinary layman. It is hoped that in this way a great deal of the difficulty which we now find in interpreting the Act may be avoided.

speakerposition: stagedirection

Section agreed to.
On section 8-postponement of nomination day on death of candidate:

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: What is the change there?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
Section 42 of the present Act reads:
Whenever from unforeseen accident, delays or otherwise, the proclamation in Form No. 19 cannot be mailed as in section 37 required, or whenever any candidate dies after being nominated and before the close of the polls, the returning officer shall fix another day for the nomination of candidates, which day shall be the nearest which will admit of compliance with the requirements of said section, and shall reissue and republish in manner provided by this Act said proclamation, with such necessary changes thereof as result from the postponement of the nominations. In every such case, the returning officer shall, with his return, make to the Chief Electoral Officer a special report of the causes which occasioned such postponement.
<* _ _
This section was held to be too indefinite to be any kind of guide to the ordinary returning officer; he would not know the number of days necessary to elapse and might innocently make a mistake in fixing the new date. The new section is more definite in its terms.

Suppose a candidate
were to die the day after the election, or before the day of declaration and return,

would the returning officer have to return the dead man as elected?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Under the Act law as it has always stood, I do not think there would he anything else for him to do.

This
amendment seems to do away with the proviso "whenever from unforeseen accident, delay or otherwise", and to limit the occasion for postponement to the death of the candidate. Might not some other unforeseen accident or occurrence make a postponement necessary?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
The Chief Electoral
Officer thought that everything was pretty definitely determined by the law, and himself suggested that these words be taken out, and that the section should provide only for postponement in the case of the death of a candidate.
If it were found impossible to take the necessary steps for an election before the proper date, what would be the effect?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: We have provided for that in the general clauses.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Subsection 1 of section 52 permits each candidate to be represented by two agents or electors who are given the right to be present in the polling station. speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: The effect of subsection 1 of section 55 was to permit in certain byelections seven days to elapse between nomination and polling. The Chief Electoral Officer thinks it would be better to make it fourteen days for all elections; consequently the special provision with regard to seven days, being the last paragraph of subsection 1 of section 55, is struck out.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 11

hours of polling:
Mr; GUTHRIE: The present section provides that the polls shall be opened at the hour of six o'clock in the forenoon in urban polling divisions and be kept open until six o'clock in the afternoon, and that in rural polling divisions the polls shall be kept open from eight o'clock in the forenoon until six o'clock in the afternoon. The practical experience has been that few if any votes have been cast before eight o"clock in the morning; the officials have been in their places, but the voters have not come forward to vote. The committee thought, therefore, that the change embodied in the present amendment would be satisfactory to all persons concerned.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I think it was suggested last year that the hour of opening should be eight instead of six. This change, like several others, follows the recommendation made from this side.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: We will give my hon. friend credit for it, then, I do not remember it.

There is not the slightest necessity in rural districts of opening polls at eight o'clock and closing them at six o'clock; all votes can be polled between the hours of nine and five, and in those districts where there is not a very large number of voters, from nine and five is a long enough time to stay at the polls. I do not speak now about cities or towns where men are at their work and may want to go to the polls at a later or an earlier hour. In rural districts, the old law of opening the polls at nine and closing at five was very satisfactory.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
It has been said-I do not know whether there is much foundation for the statement or not-that the hours are too short in the rural sections of Ontario, for instance, in certain rural polls where perhaps <350 votes may be cast. Time is not allowed for casting all the votes if voter after voter is challenged. In fact, many representations were
4 p.m. made, prior tp the last referendum in Ontario, that the hours of polling should be extended, if possible. There is also power in rural districts to add names at the polls,, and that takes a little time. For those reasons, it would be well to keep to the hours of nine in the morning to six at night. Although I myself preferred the old method of opening at nine in the rhorning and closing at five in the afternoon, on account of the extra oath that may be administered it is necessary to give a little more time. We can see how this works out at a general election.

I notice the period
between nomination and polling day is extended from seven to fourteen days all around. Has any corresponding change been made as regards the completion of the lists? There was some fixed time before polling day when lists had to be completed. Can the minister from memory tell me when the lists must be completed? Must they be completed before nomination day?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
That has not been
changed in any way. I could not from memory state the number of days. A tremendous number of calculations of time are involved, and while the Chief Electoral Officer has them at his finger ends, I have not. The only change in the section to which my hon. friend refers would affect certain by-elections. The Act of last session provided that in certain by-elections where there were lists, only seven days should elapse between nomination day and polling day. The general provision in the Act is that in all elections the period should be fourteen days. The effect of the present amendment is to make the fourteen-day period applicable to all elections, whether general or by-elections. Consequently, all the calculations of time that would apply with respect to the fourteen-day period, will apply under this amendment as well as under the Act of last session.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.

On section 12-name, address and occupation corresponding closely to another.

At what stage of the
proceedings is a man called upon t6 take this very drastic oath? A man may be mistaken as to his qualifications. In the province from which I come, a man's name appears on the list, and it is taken for granted that he is a qualified voter. This sounds a little drastic-that a man should swear that he is qualified. He may make a mistake; there may be some property disqualification of which he knows nothing. This is a very far-reaching oath.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
I can only say that
my hon. friend's friends in the committee insisted on this oath. The objection which they took to this Bill was that this oath was not in the former legislation. I do not think the oath is any more drastic than the ordinary oath. A man who makes a mistake, if his mistake was a bona fide one, could hardly be chargeable, taking an oath of this kind, with committing the offence of taking an improper oath. In order that he may be so chargeable, the offence must be wilful and corrupt.
It might be presumed to be done maliciously.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
It might be; but all
the oaths attached to the schedule to this legislation are equally strong in language, and they are drawn with the idea of making them as strong as they can be made. This oath was insisted upon by hon. gentlemen opposite in the committee; a legal gentleman, whom they had present as an expert, dwelt particularly on this oath, and the committee agreed that it should be inserted. The object of this clause, as pointed out by the Chief Electoral Officer, is that:
There is no provision made in the Act for an oath to be sworn by a person who applies to vote and whose name, address and occupation is almost but not quite identical with a name, address and occupation appearing on the voters' list ; in other words, no provision is made to meet the case of clerical or like errors made by a. registrar or revising officer. When provincial lists were used at Dominion elections the procedure in such cases was ordinarily governed by the provincial laws, but now that special Dominion lists are always prepared, the Dominion Elections Aot should, it Would appear, specify a procedure to be followed. The insertion of a new section as section 57 A, and of a new oath as Form 32 A, in the following terms would meet the case.

I can
see that that is a very necessary provision, but some difficulty might arise. Suppose the names of two men are similar. Let us say

that the name on the list is "John McDonald," and a man called John J. McDonald comes to vote on "that name; he takes the oath, and he says that he is qualified. There is only a slight difference between the two names. When the real John McDonald turns up in a few minutes and wants to vote, what becomes of him?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
The Chief Electoral
Officer points out to me that the same difficulty would exist in regard to any name. Suppose the name "John Smith" is on the list, and a man comes along and says: "I am John Smith," and he swears to that. The thing has happened. The real John Smith may come along after this, and somebody has voted for him.

Is he
debarred from voting?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
In a rural division he
certainly could vote by taking the oath. In an urban division there is also a special provision and a special oath to cover the case cited by my hon. friend.

Then
they would both vote?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
Yes. The man would
have to take a special oath.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 13-application for recount on re-addition by judge:

Do I understand this to mean that there may be a recount after the candidate has been declared elected? Did not the old law provide that the candidate must apply for a recount before the declaration day? It seems extraordinary that a man should be declared elected, a recount take place, and that he be declared elected again.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
My information is that prior to the Act of last session there could be no recount until somebody had been declared elected. It was provided that, so many days after the declaration, the party aggrieved could apply for a recount, but until somebody was declared elected no application for a recount could be entertained. The provision here is that an application for a recount shall be made within four days after the declaration. The amendment goes further and provides that in cases where the judge has territorial jurisdiction over several ridings, in case there may be two or three applications to him for a recount, he shall take them in the order in which they come to him, and further,
where one riding extends into two or three territorial jurisdictions of judges, provision here is made as to the judge to whom application shall be made. These were omissions in the Act of last session which we desire to clear up.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
I think the question of an improper addition is covered by the language of this section. It says:.
If within four days after the day on which the returning officer has declared a candidate elected it is made to appear, on the affidavit of a credible witness, to the judge hereafter described, that a deputy returning officer in counting" the votes-
It is the deputy that does the counting.
-has improperly counted or improperly rejected-
That is, refused to count
-any ballot papers or has made an incorrect statement of the number of ballots cast for any candidate-
Would not that cover everything?

I think probably that
last would cover it.

Is not this a new
section altogether as compared with the election law before the 1917 War-time Elections Act? I think the old law was entirely different.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
I do not think it was
different. This was taken from the old section No., 193.

I think the old law
contained provision for an appeal to the Supreme Court judge, but as I heard the Chairman read this section, I did not hear any such provision.

The last two lines provide
that "all such recounts or re-additions shall proceed continuously from day to day until the last of them has been completed." Does that mean that there can be no postponement for any cause whatsoever?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: I think the judge would always have jurisdiction to grant any reasonable postponement. That would be considered a proceeding from day to day.

An adjournment by the
judge?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 14-report by returning officer: *

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: The section as it appears in the Act requires the returning officer to make a report as to the state of the ballot boxes or ballot papers as received by him. Now the returning officer, if he does his duty, never sees the ballot papers except in the case of a recount, and it appears likely that the clause was intended to refer to the election papers as received from deputy returning officers. The repeal of the subsection and its re-enactment in its present form is to prevent a misconception.

Section 2, subsection
(f) of the Act defines the words "election papers" to mean all ballot papers including unused ballot books, lists of voters, and other documents used at a polling station. These words would therefore include ballots as well as the books kept at the different polls.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
In subsection (1) of
section 72, paragraph (b) of the Act as it stands, the returning officer, immediately after the election, is required to transmit by registered post to the Chief Electoral Officer a return of his proceedings, which return shall contain such observations as he may think proper as to the state of the ballot boxes or the ballot papers as received by him. Now, the term "election papers" includes ballot papers, but, as pointed out by the Chief Electoral Officer, the returning officer will never see the ballot papers. The deputy is the man who sees them put into the boxes. He seals the boxes and they are all forwarded to the returning officer with the other returns described under the term "election papers".

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.

On section 15-penalty for voting if disqualified, not qualified or incompetent

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
This section contains
a provision which was omitted from the Act of last session. In the opinion of the committee it should be inserted now.

I notice, in section 64, subsection 2, of the Act, provision is made for the laying of information, while there is no punishment meted out, and I am not sure that in some cases punishment should be inflicted. We saw in the referendum in our province, perhaps more clearly than we should see in a General election, what would be the effect of the application of this section if it were applied to all sorts of elections, such as that particular one. If the section were applied to referendum elections some unreasonable things might occur. For instance, though the referendum vote was province-wide, and affected every person in every constituency, many persons under the Act were shut out. This happened in the case of people living on the border line between two constituencies. I know of a girl, a teacher, whose home was in the town of Woiseley. She had lived there up to a short time before the election, but was not residing there at the time, having crossed the river Qu'Appelle to teach in a neighbouring school. According to the Act she was not entitled to vote anywhere, although as a matter of fact, I believe, the registrar in the polling district where she was living at the time of the election, put her name on the list without application on her part. Suppose that girl had voted, would she have been liable to imprisonment under this Act? It seems to me that a great many cases of that kind may and will occur. I believe that most of the offences that will be tried under the Act, under the provision that prohibits a person from voting where he is not entitled to vote, will be committed by those who feel they have a moral right to vote where they do vote, although technically they might be shut out. When a person finds himself accidentally on the voters' list in a district where he is living at the time of the election, even though he has not been living in the district the required length of time prior to the election, he will be tempted to vote, and it is not very probable that people generally will be aware of the provision of the Act which makes it an indictable offence to exercise what they may believe to be a moral right. Perhaps the minister will tell us what the effect would be if a person were placed on the

list, without his application, in a rural polling division where he lived, and he went in and voted. Would he be guilty of an indictable offence?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: I cannot see what wrong he would be doing. In the first place, in a rural poll, he would have a right to vote on polling day.

Not necessarily. I
am supposing a case where he had not the technical right to vote because he had come in from an adjoining constituency. There may be something more to be said in favour of punishing a voter in the case of a general election than in the case of a referendum. But suppose a person goes across the boundary line and, not having lived two months in the rural district where he desires to vote, he finds his name on the voters' 'list, although he had taken no part whatever in having it placed there. It is the most natural thing in the world that under such circumstances he would want to vote. If he did so, would he be guilty of an indictable offence?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: In that case, I understand, he does not take the oath at all.
No.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Well, uniless he deliberately and intentionally seeks to do a wrong in voting when he knows he is not entitled to voted, I do not think he would be liable to punishment. I grant that in the working out of this Act, particularly in endeavouring to apply it to the Canada Temperance Act, there were considerable difficulties to be overcome. But it was thought by this House to be far better to apply the Act than to pass new and elaborate machinery to take a single referendum. The difficulty which my hon. friend points out in Saskatchewan and Alberta was overcome in the province of Ontario by an amendment which we passed during the first weeks of this session. We allowed the provincial franchise in Ontario, so that a man, notwithstanding thet he was on the list for the city of Toronto, could vote in the city of Ottawa if he had been here two months; and if he went to a rural poll, he could vote in any case, no matter in what part of the province he resided, so long as he could swear that he had been two months resident in Ontario. When the votes were taken in the western provinces on the referendum, this difficulty was not anticipated and considerable inconvenience arose in consequence.

Perhaps I am taking up too much time over this, but I think there will be some difference of opinion as to the meaning of some of these clauses. This section, for instance, speaks of a person who votes or attempts to vote, knowing that he is for any reason disqualified, non-qualified, or incompetent to vote. Now, a person whose name has been placed on the voters' list may say he is not disqualified. He is not non-qualified or non-competent because his name is on the list and he has been asked to vote, but would he, because he was a few days short of the time, be liable to criminal prosecution by reason of voting when his name was placed on the list without any request of his own.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: I do not see how any man could get his name on the list without any request of his own, under this law. In the first place the rural enumerator takes as a basis the provincial list where there is one that is not more than two years old. There is a provision, in addition, for a man to apply to get his name on. How then does somebody else get this fellow's name on the list?

I am talking of the
practice-in our part of the country. I do not think that, we have, in the rural parts of Saskatchewan-but as to that I am not sure-any list to start with. I think the general practice is for the registrar or enumerator in the first place to make out a list of voters in the polling district. He knows that a certain person is living in the district, and he thinks that person is entitled to vote and he puts his name on the list. The person in question sees his name on the list and very naturally says "I am not disqualified, I am not nonqualified, I am not non-competent, for they have put my name on the list. Therefore I vote."

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: I doubt very much whether any one could prosecute that man.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 16-voting on advanced polls.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Is there any change there?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
Under subsections 9 and 10 of section 100 as it now stands, certificates entitling a voter to vote at an advanced poll may be issued at any polling division by the registrar or the revising officer. Both urban and rural registrars are thus entitled to issue these certificates, although the urban registrar prepares only

a preliminary list which may be substantially changed by the revising officer. Transfer certificates, under section 53, can be issued only by the revising officer in urban polling divisions, but a corresponding limitation with respect to certificates to voters at advanced polls would prevent possible irregularities. This would involve the repeal of section 100 subsection 9, paragraph (a) and the first line of section 100, subsection 10, and of the substitution therefor of the following, -the amendments being indicated in italics. Then in the Bill we have the amendments suggested.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 17-issue of certificate gratis to applicant for vote at advanced poll.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: That is just consequent on the last section.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 18-attendance of officers and notice of time and place.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: That is for the general information and convenience of those persons entitled to vote at advanced polls.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 19-no amendment to apply to election for which writ is issued within three months, except after notice.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
This is by way of safeguard in order to provide time for the necessary printing to be done in case amendments are made by Parliament at any session and an election held shortly thereafter. The note I have from the chief electoral officer is as follows:
Amendments of the Act often, indeed almost always, involve change in the forms and instructions, and if they go into force suddenly, upon receiving the Royal assent, grave inconvenience might arise and irregularities ensue by reason of the use in an immediately following election of forms and instructions for the reprinting of which the interval was insufficient. Tihe insertion in section 102 of the following is recommended to cover this point and authorize consolidation of amendments to the Act.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to. -
On section 20-new forms substituted.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
The reason for this is that it was found, notwithstanding the care that was exercised in the preparation of the forms last session when the Act was passed, that there were very important clerical errors in the forms, some of them very serious and some maybe exceedingly misleading. In the interval the forms have been thoroughly revised, 
and we think all such irregularities, all such clerical errors, have now been eliminated. The proposal is, and it has met with the hearty approval of the committee, that the forms should be re-enacted.
All of them?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
All of them, in order that we may get rid of the old forms, which were open to a good deal of doubt, and have an entirely new set, and that is the object of the next two sections. There is one other form which is even omitted in this compilation and which the Chief Electoral Officer has handed to me. Perhaps I can deal with it now. It will be known as "Form No. 29" under section 53, "the form of oath in Transfer Certificate." It is apparently the ordinary oath but was omitted in the book. This is to take the place of the one in the old Act which the Chief Electoral Officer says is inadequate. The form of oath is as follows:
Form No. 29 (S. 53)
Oath on Transfer 'Certificate ^ I, (Name) of (address) (occupation) do swear (or affirm) that:
1.	I am the person described in the transfer
certificate which I produce authorizing me to vote in Polling Division No.	instead of
in the Polling Division No.	in the electoral district of	:
2.	I am a British subject of the full age of
twenty-one years and have ordinarily resided in Canada for the year and in this electoral district for the two months immediately preceding the	day of	19	,
(naming the date of the issue of the writ of election).
3.	I am not within any of the classes of persons who lack qualification or are disqualified by reason of appointment to judicial office, employment for pay or reward in reference to the election, place of birth, race, crime, mental incapacity, the receipt of public charitable support or disfranchisement for corrupt or illegal practices.
4.	I have not already voted at this election and have not been guilty of any corrupt or illegal practice in relation thereto, So Help Me God.
Sworn (or affirmed) before me at the polling station for polling division No.	this	dayof	, 19	.
Deputy Returning Officer.
This is the oath which applies to those persons who vote on transfer certificates, scrutineers, and the like.
On the schedule.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Have all
these forms been approved by the Chief Electoral Officer and by the Committee on Privileges and Elections?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Yes, they have all been drawn by the Chief Electoral Officer and approved by the committee unanimously. Form 29 is the one I read.

Speaking as a member of the Committee on Privileges and Elections, I do not remember that we ever went over all these forms. We took the word of the Chief Electoral Officer and of the minister that the forms were consistent with the Act, and that the changes made in them were merely so that the forms would dovetail-to use the minister's expression-in with the Act itself. But I should not like the committee to receive the impression that the Committee on Privileges and Elections had really worked [DOT]over these forms.
If not you ought to have done so.
Before we go on with the schedules, Mr. Chairman, am I in order in proposing an additional clause?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member would certainly be in order in proposing an additional clause now, but as we have already started on the schedule, and as I understand the minister desires to dispose of clause 3, if the hon. member will allow the present amendment to be proceeded with he will have an opportunity later to move his additional clause.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: I beg to move that the section be amended by striking out Form 29 and substituting therefor the form which I have just submitted.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Amendment agreed to.
Schedule as amended agreed to.
On motion of Mr. Guthrie the committee returned to the consideration of section 3- revising officers.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
Under the Elections
Act passed last session judges would certainly have been entitled to fees but for the provisions of the Judges Act. Under that Act it has been held that a judge performing services during an election could not receive fees. The judges have performed a lot of pretty hard work in this connection, and it has been suggested to the Chief Electoral Officer-not to the Government or any member of it-that they might receive reasonable remuneration for such services. The Chief Electoral Officer points out that if Parliament wants the lists to be revised by judges provision for payment will have to be made, and that if we do not make
such provision the greater part of the lists will be revised by substitutes appointed by the judges.

Who would be
lawyers?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Yes; but the substitutes will be paid. If it is the desire of the House to utilize the services of judges for this work, I fancy that as a practical matter we will have to make provision for their payment. A judge has power under the Act to appoint substitutes, and it is absolutely necessary that that power be given because in many ridings, such as Toronto, Montreal, and the like, a judge cannot do all the work and substitutes are a necessity. If the judges find they are not going to receive anything for their labours, they will not work any harder and substitutes will be appointed. Personally I do not favour paying judges, and it is a suggestion made by the Chief Electoral Officer for the working out of the Act. Whatever the committee decides will be agreeable to the Government.

My hon. friend does not state in so many words that the judges, although paid servants of the country, will not do their duty under this Act unless paid extra, but that is the implication. I am quite willing to have our judges well paid-and I have supported every proposal to increase their salaries-but I hope the suggestion is not justified that they, who should he the highest exemplars of good citizenship, will not do their work without receiving extra pay, although they are already paid liberal salaries. If we want the judges to do this work, it is part of the public service for which they are already paid, and they have no right to receive extra payment for it.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
We have not placed
this as an obligation on the judges; they have the option under the Act of doing it or not doing it. The idea I intended to convey was that if they get nothing for their services they will probably appoint substitutes to do the work, and those substitutes will have to he paid; hut if the provision in this amendment were to pass, judges doing the work would receive the same remuneration as their substitutes.
I think my hon. friend can provide that it is incumbent on a judge to do this work in so far as his other duties will permit him, but where that is not the case he will be allowed to appoint

speakerposition: subtopic
stagedirection
speechtext: a substitute. I am obliged to repeat my former observation that the time a judge devotes to this work is time for which he is already paid.

I do not quite agree with my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's in respect to what should properly be regarded as the duties of judges. The duty of a judge in administering the law is a part of his profession, and he certainly should not get any extra payment for the discharge of that duty; but when we take him away from that and ask him to do work that has nothing to do with his calling or training as a lawyer, we are asking him to do something which his salary as a judge is not intended to cover at all. The minister has not said anything about the point I raised in regard to those salaries. There must be substitutes, and there is no provision made for their payment in the amendment read by the Chairman. If an account came to the hands of the Auditor General for payment of such work, I think he would be disposed to say, "there is no provision under this Act for passing this account." If this provision for paying a judge is made to read that it shall also apply to the man he appoints in his place, I think it would very much simplify matters, and we would not be troubled with what construction a taxing officer might put upon the law. If the judges are called upon to do work which is outside their regular duties they should be paid for it just as anybody else would be paid for it.
But a judge who does that work is devoting his time to a service which has no relation whatever to his duties of office.
But he has to do the other work as well.
Will this provision apply in the case of judges who issue voting certificates under section 29?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
Under the present
iariff, framed under section 76, the whole fee to which a judge or his substitute would be entitled, for doing all the work in connection with an election would be $50.

It would seem to be the general policy of the House to avoid extra payments to judges, and to let them depend on the salaries which we vote them. I think there is a great deal in the contention of the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's that when we assign

a salary to a judge we are paying him for such time as he is able to give to the service of the country. I know, and the minister himself knows, that there are some judges who have not much to do, but who get the same salaries as those who have twice as much to do; I think that is why the minister himself is not wholly in favour of his amendment. Some judges have very little to do; others have too much to do. In the case of the judge whose duties are so great that he has no time to give to such services as these, it is well that we should have a provision enabling him to engage some one else to do it. But where the judge himself does the work-and a great many of them will feel that they themselves should do it-I do not think they should be given extra pay, because if that judge has not enough work to do there is no reason why he should not give gratis the time for these duties. There is no reason why the judge who has only half enough work to keep him busy should get extra pay which the busy man is not in a position to get. I think, therefore, that the amendment should be voted down.

Every province has
its set times and places for holding courts in all districts. The time for the opening and closing of the court is set. The judges must hold chambers on certain days of the week. The judges must have time to keep abreast of their profession and thus be enabled to discharge properly their duties as judges. But you cannot put judges out at statute labour between times; you cannot send them to follow threshing mills and do that sort of thing. That is not their business. They are called upon to do certain work at certain times and outside of that we have no claim on their time.

I agree
with the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's. The judges should be well paid. I think that since I have been in this house we have twice increased the salaries of judges. If those salaries are not sufficiently high we should increase them still further. But I do object to any particular class of people having their salaries increased indirectly through fees and commissions and things of that kind. I notice, of course, the very earnest manner in which the lawyers of the House come to the defence of the judges, not only on this occasion but on every occasion. I am not saying they should not, because they all

have prospective judgeships in mind, I presume.
Perish the thought!

Order.
Mr. McGIBBON ^Muskoka):	I think
the principle is bad, Mr. Chairman. I do not think that judges, especially judges of the county court in Ontario, are worked very hard. In fact, any of them with whose work I happen to be acquainted have a very easy time. Some of them hold court three or four times a year, three or four days each time, and they are quite free not only to leave their districts at times, but occasionally to leave the province and sometimes the country for long periods.
That is because the doctor orders complete rest.

I hope my hon. friend will have a very considerate physician when he reaches that stage. As I say, the principle is absolutely wrong. The judges are certainly supposed to give all their time to the country's interest, and if these matters come under their jurisdiction I do not think they should receive extra pay.
