Before the Bill goes out
of committee I would like to suggest the addition of a clause, amending section 29 of the Dominion Elections Act of last year. I directed the attention of the minister and of the Government last year to what I thought was an injustice in connection with the disfranchisement of certain citizens. At that time the Government gave us an amendment which corrected the wrong to some extent but which in my opinion did not go far enough. Believing as I do that a thing is not settled until it is settled right, I am going to suggest to the minister the addition of a clause which will remove entirely what I believe to be an injustice to a large number of Canadian citizens.
I should like to explain briefly the significance of the clause to which I take exception, subsection 2 of section 29. It is that all women of alien origin who are married to British subjects and by virtue of that marriage have themselves become British subjects are not given the vote as are their sister British subjects in this country, without being put to the necessity of appearing before a judge to whom they must show cause why they should be granted a voting certificate. In effect,
197J
while it is possible for these women to obtain voting privileges, the provision results in the practical disfranchisement of 100,000 or more people who are citizens of Canada under the law. I want to suggest that the conferring of citizenship should carry with it the franchise without unnecessary restrictions. In my opinion the min-, ister offered no convincing reason last year why an exception should be made in the case of these women. To-day we have a condition whereby not only women of former enemy alien origin but women who come from France or Belgium or Italy or Russia, if they are married to Canadian citizens and have thus become British subjects, are debarred from voting if they do not go to the trouble of appearing before a judge. I will admit frankly that a good many people in my constituency are affected by this. I think many more are affected in the western provinces. I would again urge upon the minister to go the whole length of removing this grievance and of allowing British citizenship to carry with it the right to vote. Under the British law, so soon as a woman marries a British citizen, she herself becomes a British subject. She should by right have the vote as have other women who are citizens of Canada.
One other point has, perhaps, been lost sight of. Under the law, when a man of foreign origin becomes naturalized, the minor children of that man also become British subjects, and in the past, on attaining the proper age, they have been allowed to vote. Under the law as it now stands, even those men who, perhaps, for many years have been voting, are put to the necessity of appearing before a judge and obtaining a voting certificate. That is wrong; it is an indignity to those people; it is not fair. Practically the only privilege that goes with British citizenship is the right of the ballot, and this Government should not place itself in the position of giving citizenship with one hand and taking away the greatest privilege of citizenship with the other. For that reason, I move that the following clause be added to the Bill as clause 22 thereof:
22. "Sulbsection (2) of section 29 of the Dominion Elections Act, chapter forty-six of the Statutes of 1920, is hereby repealed."

I take it from the remarks of my hon. friend (Mr. Euler) that the intention of the amendment is to make provision by which any woman, it matters not from where she comes, who marries a British subject, shall at the moment be entitled to the franchise

in Canada. Am I right in my interpretation of the hon. gentleman's proposition?
If she fulfils the other conditions.

Under
that condition the native of an enemy country, who has been in Canada long enough to become a British citizen, who returns to the country of his origin, who marries a citizen of that country and who immediately returns to Canada, will automatically create a new elector in this country. If we take the ground that a woman gets the franchise merely by right of her husband having the franchise, there might be something in what the hon. member says; but I think all will agree that when we granted the franchise to women, we felt that we were giving the franchise to an independent body of electors who would be themselves responsible for the position that they took when they cast ballots, who would themselves decide which side of the question they were going to vote on. I do not think my hon. friend would argue that a woman, coming into this country from Eastern or Central Europe, one of the enemy countries, if you will, or for that matter, any other country, who has no idea whatever of what the ideals of Canadian citizenship are, who has never had an opportunity of understanding what they are, who simply becomes the wife of a man who, perhaps, was born in Canada and who understands them, automatically, by reason of her marriage, becomes a British citizen entitled to the franchise in Canada.

Would my hon. friend say the same thing of a Mexican woman who marries a Canadian citizen, a British subject? Should she be entitled to vote? She is, under the Act, and so is a negress from the West Indies, but a woman from France, Belgium, Italy or Germany is not.

My personal opinion would be, if the hon. member wants that, that no man or woman, who comes from any country, the ideals of whose citizenship are wholly different from or opposed to the ideals of Canadian citizenship, is competent to exercise the franchise in this country, until he or she has lived here long enough to understand something of what Canadian citizenship means. There is in the Act a provision that makes a difference for citizens of North American countries because it is recognized that people born on the North American continent have ideals largely the same as ours.
Is it because they are born on this continent that they have similar ideals?

Because they are trained here, because they are educated here, because they live under conditions similar to those that we have. That cannot be said of citizens of Eastern and Central Europe. I think my hon. friends will agree with that, and I will not labour the point. My position is simply this: I am wholly opposed to the idea behind the suggestion that, merely because a woman, coming from an enemy country or, for that matter, a friendly country, whose ideals are wholly different from ours, marries a man who is entitled to the franchise in Canada, she shall receive the franchise. In the first place, such a proposition is a direct contradiction of everything underlying the granting of the franchise to women. If a woman is to vote simply because her husband has a vote, you are simply giving the man two votes; you are not setting up an independent body of electors, and that was the idea behind the whole question of granting the franchise to women. At this time, during the years following the war, during 1920 and 1921, large numbers of men from the newer parts of Canada are going back to the countries of their origin; a very large number of them will return with their wives, newly married. These men may have been living in Canada for many years; they may know something of Canadian citizenship; but it cannot be argued that, because of that fact, their wives know something of Canadian citizenship. Their wives, if they receive the franchise, will be, in political affairs, mere automatons registering the opinions of their husbands. I do not think the hori. gentleman can offer anything in the nature of a sound argument for the granting of the franchise to a woman solely because her husband has the franchise.

The arguments of my hon. friend may be very convincing to himself, but I am sure they are not convincing to any one who has given the subject any consideration at all. He deals entirely with an exceptional case and there is no reason why the exceptional case which he suggests should not go before a judge, get a certificate
5 p.m. and vote. The only difference is that the applicant is put to some trouble. He must surely see that the exceptional case which he suggests is not touched by this at all. Another exceptional

case is put up to him, but he ignores it entirely. Is a woman coming from France, who is not permitted to vote under this legislation, any worse than a woman coming under similar conditions from Mexico? My hon. friend does not care to deal with that. That is exactly the position of the Act as it stands at present. That is what he is defending. He puts up an exceptional case, and the Act does not touch the exceptional case at all because the woman to whom he objects to give the franchise can vote under this Act. All that my hon. friend (Mr. Euler) is asking for is that a woman should not he put to unreasonable trouble, and I think he is right in his contention. I do not think the circumstances in his constituency are as had as they are in others. I know, in many parts of the West, this will simply mean shutting out from voting women who have lived in the West for the last thirty or forty years and who have become thoroughly good Canadian citizens.

Can
these women not go before the judge and qualify the same as their husbands?

Certainly, and so can people coming from alien enemy countries. Don't shut these people out at all; if they want to go before the judge, let them go. I think that you will find that the bigger proportion of the crooks who want to do some harm to the country-Reds, if you like, thorough Bolshevists, who want to upset the instir tutions of this country-will go to the judge and get the right to vote, while the honest, hard-working woman who thinks of her home, and is a good citizen, will not go as a rule. That will be the effect of the law as it stands now.

or less intelligent, cannot possibly vote against the resolution of my hon. friend from North Waterloo (Mr. Euler) without having to explain to their electors and the country at large their reasons for doing so.

I am
ready to admit my denseness, but I must nevertheless say that what I have heard from my hon. friend from Qu'Appelle (Mr. Thomson) and my hon. friend from George Etienne Cartier (Mr. Jacobs) has not converted me, but rather has it convinced me that I was right in the first place. As to what my hon. friend has said with regard to women from Mexico, if he wants my personal opinion, I am opposed to giving the franchise automatically to a man or woman from any country, I care not which, who does not understand something of the ideals of Canadian citizenship. If the provision in the Act is wrong that makes it possible for a Mexican woman to have that right, I would hold up both hands for amending the law and making it impossible for her to have that right.
Wherein do the ideals of French citizenship differ from those of Canadian citizenship?
I do not know that they differ at all, but one thing I know, and that is that the language of the average French citizen is different from the language of many Canadian citizens.

French is an official
language in this country, and in this House.

I appreciate fully what is in my hon. friend's mind. I know we have a dual language system, and I have no objection to it in any sense whatever. But that does not answer the argument at all. The whole argument in favour of granting the franchise to women because their husbands have the franchise is based on the supposition that the woman automatically becomes a British subject because her husband is. Now, becoming a British subject does not carry with it the right of the franchise; there is no question about that.
It should.

But it does not. What underlies this whole question is simply this:	When the franchise
was granted to women I think it was recognized by those who advocated it that the women were going to be an independent body of electors, exercising their own judg-

ment and having their own opinions, and not simply following the opinions and judgments of their husbands. My hon. friend says that because a man goes before a judge and takes the oath of allegiance and becomes a British subject, he can then marry any woman he pleases and she automatically becomes an elector.

She should not have to
go before the court; that is onr objection.

She should have to go; there is no reason why she should not qualify the same as a man. If it is necessary for a man to undertake certain obligations and possess certain qualifications in order to become an elector in this country, it is necessary that the woman who is exercising the same franchise and has equal privileges and responsibilities should be in identically the same position as the man, and that is what the Act calls for.

When my hon. friend
from North Waterloo (Mr. Euler) brought this matter before the House a year ago, when the Franchise Act was under discussion, I supported the position he took then, and I am very glad to support it again to-day notwithstanding the arguments that have been advanced by my hon. friend from East Algoma (Mr. Nicholson).
There may be something said for this position: that the woman coming to Canada in the future and marrying a Canadian citizen should be required by personal naturalization to qualify for the right of exercising the franchise, but there is absolutely no defence for the position of affairs resulting from the existing section in the Act which my hon. friend from North Waterloo wishes to have repealed. We have, not single isolated cases, not scores, not hundreds, not thousands, but tens of thousands of cases in this country, of women who have been living in Canada, some of them for as long as fifty years, who are disqualified under this section from voting until they have secured, often with very great difficulty, the necessary certificate from a judge.
Can these women not go before a judge and get the right to become elected?
Why should they, have to do that?
Why should a man have to do it?
He does not have to go before the judge.
He has to go before the judge to he naturalized.

Let me cite an illustration. An American citizen, a person who owed allegiance to the United States, came to Canada, say, in 1900, bringing with him his wife. He qualified in due time as a British subject, and secured the right to exercise the franchise. By that very act his wife has always been recognized in Canada, up to the present time, as a British subject. There is no question as to his right to vote, because he has qualified. Now, according to this Act, his wife must go through all this formality-
No.

Pardon me; it is one of the anomalies of the Bill that it does not apply to a woman born in America; I am taking the wrong case. But let us take the case of a French woman or an Icelandic woman," or a Norwegian, or a Swedish woman-and we have thousands of these people in the country. These women have to go personally before a judge and comply with all this formality in order to be able to exercise the franchise.
So has the man.

No. The man has been a British subject and his wife has been recognized as a British subject in this country for years, but there is a discrimination against the woman, in this section of the Act, that should not exist. As my hon. friend from George Etienne Cartier (Mr. Jacobs), and my hon. friend from Qu'-Appelle (Mr. Thomson), pointed out, a Mexican woman coming to Canada is not under the disability that has been placed upon the French woman or any of the others I have mentioned.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Mexican women do not come, as a matter of fact.
They may not, but they can, as a matter of law, and my hon. friend knows they can. It is not an argument to say that they do not, for the law expressly provides that they can come.
And so can a coloured woman from Georgetown.

Yes. Such a woman can marry a Canadian citizen and by that fact she is entitled to the franchise without going through this formality. Why place this discrimination on these other women? There are thousands of Icelandic women in Western Canada, born in Iceland, some as
long as fifty or so years ago. They have been living here, claiming and exercising all the rights of British citizenship, and yet, under this provision, they are not qualified to vote, while their husbands may have been qualified for a generation. That is not a desirable condition of affairs. If the minister in charge of the Bill drew the line at the present time and said that henceforth every alien woman coming to Canada, whether from the United States, from Mexico, Iceland, Germany, Russia, or anywhere else, must personally naturalize and qualify for the franchise, something could be said to support that position. But this discrimination should not be continued, and I suggest to my hon. friend that he might very well settle the matter in that way, which, I believe, would be entirely acceptable to the hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler). What is complained of is the disability placed under this section upon women who have been in Canada for perhaps two generations. That is wrong and should be remedied, and I think my hon. friend from North Waterloo has stated in very reasonable terms a perfectly fair proposition to the Committee.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The question which I should like to have answered in connection with this subject is, how a woman is to go before a judge if there is no judge before whom to go. That is the real problem presented by the Act as it stands at the present time. In many constituencies there are only three or four judicial centres, and in order for a large majority of women electors to become entitled to vote under the law, they have to go some ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, and in some cases, one hundred miles, to obtain the voting certificate. That is a physical impossibility, and very costly in the case of a large number of citizens. That is a feature of the Act that requires to be looked into. I made the suggestion earlier, in regard to another section of the Act, that the Committee on Privileges and Elections might be asked to consider one or two of these features of the Aet, and report upon them to the House before the close of the session. I should like the minister to consider that suggestion in regard to this amendment; if he cannot accept the amendment outright, the Committee on Privileges and Elections might look into this particular matter in view of the injustice which it occasions to thousands of women electors who are about to exercise the franchise now for the first time. Un-

fortunately, there is not in Parliament any woman to voice the women's point of view on this disability as women see it. Happily, however, I happen to have here an article which has been written by a woman who has given careful study to this particular section of the Act, and which presents in a manner that I think will appeal to hon. members, the real nature of the difficulty involved in the section as it stands, and the great injustice which it does not to hundreds but to thousands of women who are British subjects in this country. The article in question appears in the Manitoba Free Press of May 2, and is written by Miss Mary P. McCallum, assistant secretary to the Canadian Council of Agriculture. I shall not read the whole article, but the part that relates to the point brought up by my hon. friend from Qu'Appelle, where he spoke of the inconvenience to which numbers of electors are put, and the unnecessary trouble which is entailed upon them in consequence of this section. The article says:
The most serious difficulty is that of the inaccessibility of judges to most rural residents in the prairie provinces. There are not more than one or two judicial centres in each federal riding. In one at least, Last Mountain, there is no court centre. Each judge has an itinerary of three or four places in his judicial district where he holds district court once or twice a year. The court sits at these points usually for not more than a day. The majority of persons who require these certificates reside scores of miles from any place where the judge is scheduled to hold court. Railways are not convenient which may require an awkward change of trains, long delays, hotel expense, etc.
Hon. members will see from that statement that women under the Act as it stands now have to know, first of all, the one day of the year on which a judge may be at a particular centre, and then may have to travel hundreds of miles in order to get the voting certificate. I am sure that if hon. members appreciated the real nature of the working of this section of the Act, they would not willingly inflict this injustice on a large number of British subjects. Take a concrete instance, which is the next point mentioned in the article, of the by-election which will be held in Medicine Hat in the near future. Here is the exact statement as to how the Act will operate in connection with this one byelection :
This may be illustrated by taking the case of Medicine Hat. There is to be a by-election there some time this summer to fill the vacancy created by the death of the late Hon. A. L. Sifton. There are parts of three judicial districts in Medicine Hat, but in all, the judge holds court at only five points in the entire

riding, which is 192 miles long and 66 miles wide. Three railways run east and west across the constituency. A woman at Iddesleigh at the western edge of the riding on the Empress-Bassano branch of the Canadian Pacific railway, enquired where she must go for her "voting certificate". She may go to Empress, 118 miles away, on June 14, when the district court sits, or to Calgary, 138 miles away; or to Medicine Hat, 148 miles distant, changing trains in either of the latter two cases. In these times the cost in money and time is prohibitory and amounts to disfranchisement.
Compared to McKenzie or Humboldt or Victoria constituencies, Medicine Hat cannot be said to be largely a non-English constituency but the disfranchisement, in Medicine Hat is not inconsiderable.
Taking the case of women only, according to the census of 1916 there were 3,246 females in the electoral riding of Medicine Hat who were not British born. According to the same census three-fifths of them would be of voting age. This leaves about 2,000 women born in foreign countries and of voting age. In Alberta 18 per cent of the people in 1916 were born in the United States. This percentage, applied to the women in this constituency leaves something over 1,500 women of foreign birth outside the Continent of North America who must travel to one of these five points and obtain their "voting certificate" to enable them to vote in the by-election this coming spring or summer.
Now there is the case of just one constituency with respect to the pending byelections, and what is true of that constituency is more or less true of every constituency in the Canadian west, and is true in a large measure of constituencies in other parts of Canada as well. If these facts are correct-and I challenge the minister to dispute them at all-it will be apparent that this Act, instead of being an Act to enfranchise women voters, is going to disfranchise thousands of British citizens in this country. Is it any wonder, therefore, that the writer of this article concludes with the following paragraph:
The Government may deny the disfranchising effect of the Elections Act on technicality. But it disfranchises on a scale not approached by the War Time Elections Act. That Act affected the persons of enemy alien extraction, but it did not touch the Dane, or the Frenchman, or the Hollander, or the persons of any other friendly foreign country. Now, it says to all persons of foreign birth, who have been naturalized by operation of law, execpt those bom in the United States, no matter whether they have voted in this country for the last thirty or forty years, that they are no longer British subjects and may not vote until they produce evidence by a most roundabout and inconvenient method, that they are qualified to vote. Their thinking process in their adopted English is likely to get a very stubborn hold of one fact, namely, that they are disfranchised. Professions of lofty motives on the part of the Government are likely to excite still more their resentment and not to interest or mollify them at all. Unless something is done soon to re-establish their pre-war confidence in Canadian men and Canadian institutions the thin edge of the wedge of disruption already will have been driven into

the life of Western Canada. With absolute power virtually to disfranchise thousands of persons, does it look as if the next election is to be the free and unbiased opinion of the whole people of Canada upon the issues engaging the Government of the country?
I contend that that statement, which is from a woman's point of view on a matter which affects the women voters of this country, is entitled to the most careful consideration of this House. I think, on the face of it, it clearly discloses the truth of the statement that the Act, as it stands, disfranchises thousands of British subjects; and I would therefore repeat, in order that the matter may be dealt with in as thoughtful and careful a way as possible, that I think the minister would be well advised if he would allow the Committee on Privileges and Elections to take this representation, by a woman of this country, on behalf of the women of Canada, and consider this section of the Act in relation to these representations, and see if it is not possible to make some amendment which will serve the purpose which is most needed. May I point out this fact:	If it is not
possible for the minister to see his way to amending the Act, so as to prevent it being necessary for women to travel these hundreds of miles on one particular day to get a voting certificate, perhaps the law can be amended in a way that will fix a certain date by which judges would be required by itinerary to visit the different parts of these constituencies so as to give the voters there ,a chance to obtain their voting certificates. I think the Government should seek to meet the people, rather than that the people should be obliged to run after some officer of the Government in order to obtain what is the just and right privilege of every British subject.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
This question comes up before the committee rather irregularly because it forms no part of the Bill under discussion; but the leader of the Opposition intimated on the second reading of he Bill that he would like permission for he discussion of one or two amendments which were not incorporated in the measure, and for the purpose of discussion we readily agreed. However, I had not at that time any idea that this question which was so thoroughly discussed eleven months ago, was going to be re-introduced into the House again to-day. I know of no clause in the Franchise Act of last session which occupied quite as much time as the question under discussion to-day. After the most prolonged consideration
and discussion, eleven months ago, this House adopted a certain course, and I do not think that in the meantime anything has transpired to cause it to change its opinion. However, I have received a little light on the subject this afternoon from my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition -a suggestion which was not before us when the clause was considered last year- and that is that something might be done in the way of asking judges, or procuring judges, to go round the various country districts a little more than they have done in the past. This, however, must be kept clearly in mind: There have been eleven full months now during which these women could have obtained these certificates. Very few of them, I understand, have made application. They take little or no interest in the matter. They have not shown enough interest in the question to go and apply for certificates, except in very few instances-not in the West, but in the thickly populated districts in the East. Now, I can well understand that in certain of the more remote constituencies there will be some degree of inconvenience to some people. We knew that last year, we discussed it last year, and the view of the House at that time was, that notwithstanding some slight inconvenience with which a limited number of people would have to put up, the principle was nevertheless a sound one; and if it is a good principle to apply it to people coming to this country in the future, as is suggested by my hon. friend the leader of the Agrarian group (Mr. Crerar), it would be just as sound a principle to apply it to those already here.
Not at all.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
If we are going to
include all those who come in the future and require with respect to them that they shall apply to a judge, why draw a distinction between them and those who are here? Those who are here have never voted in Canada, those who are coming in future have never voted, and if one class is to be placed at some disadvantage and inconvenience so should the other class. But the inconvenience has been very much magnified here and in the matter which has been read. In the vast majority of cases there is no inconvenience at all. These people have not regarded the sacred right of the franchise very highly because, even in the county of my hon. friend (Mr. Euler) the county of Waterloo, little advantage has been taken, if any, of the

permission to obtain these certificates. Under that state of affairs I submit there is no grievance and there are no hardships; but I do not think it would be improper to suggest that some measure might be framed, particularly with respect to the more remote constituencies, whereby, within the next twelve or fifteen months, say, judges should make periodical visits to the more remote sections in order to give every facility for obtaining these certificates. However, I do not think that is a ground for amending the Dominion Elections Law. I think that matter is well worth consideration, but not in connection with this Bill-that would be in connection with the Judges Act or some other Act; and I shall have to ask the committee to vote down the amendment of my hon. friend from North Waterloo.

I cannot
agree with my hon. friend that there is anything irregular in the amendment that is proposed. The measure before us is a Bill to amend the Dominion Elections Act. It is perfectly true that the minister has put in a number of clauses of his own, but there is nothing to preclude any hon. member-

[Mr. Guthrie. 3	.

Well, he knows, as any other member knows, that the laws as passed by Parliament are not known to the electorate within a month or tiyo, or even a year or two, and that in many cases laws such as these affecting particularly the rights of persons of foreign origin are not likely ever to be heard of by them. That is not through any fault of theirs, it is their misfortune. They cannot keep themselves informed of all legislation. speechtext: No, for the purposes of holding court. Each judge, no matter where he is in his own district, can grant these certificates. Now, if the provincial authorities say that a judge shall hold court at this, that and the other point, within the next six, eight, or twelve months, that will give the people of those remote districts an opportunity to get certificates,- if there is a real grievance.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition

My hon.
friend knows that the provinces would not likely authorize or direct a judge to hold court simply for the sake of holding court.
I want to find out if my hon. friend means that a province might direct judges to visit different centres for the purpose of permitting persons to appear before them to get voting certificates, and whether it would be within its jurisdiction in instructing the judges to act accordingly?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: No. They could direct the judges to hold court at A, B, C and D for all judicial purposes; that would be sufficient.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition

My hon.
friend knows, better perhaps than any one else in the House, that that is not going to be done by any province where they have only two or three customary centres.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: We are paying for it; it does not cost the province anything. If there is a real grievance-something that has not been magnified in this House; and I maintain it has been-in these remote parts, all the local government has to do is to designate certain convenient point for the judges to hold their courts, and the judges are bound to go. We pay them their salaries and travelling expenses. There the people can appear and get the certificates that they are entitled to. That gets over the incopevnience; and it is the only thing wrong with the Act, if it is a grievance.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
To make this perfectly clear, would the attorney general of Alberta, for instance, be justified, with' the support of his government, in directing that the judges in that province should
hold court this next year, say, in forty different centres in each constituency?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence

Then I
think my hon. friend, to be fair with the House, ought to make perfectly clear what is in the back of his mind. Before that step could be taken, which on the face of it is plausible enough, it would be necessary for each province to enact legislation establishing additional courts for all purposes. That is a step the provinces might very well hesitate to take. But I do think this Government ought, in connection with the administration of this Act, to put in a clause which would meet what I am sure my hon. friend sees now is an injustice that will not bear examination.

Did I understand the
minister to say that in any case the Federal Government would pay for the costs involved in holding these additional courts?

My hon. friend knows very well. they do not do that. And this would mean, so far as the provinces are concerned, that if they were to establish the necessary number of courts to properly handle this work it would mean a great additional expense, and my hon. friend knows perfectly well they will not undertake it.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Perhaps my suggestion was too expensive.
I would like to ask my hon. friend another question. I am not a lawyer and I-

therefor.

-am asking for enlightenment. I will illustrate my question in this way. An Icelander came to Canada say, forty years ago, with a son five years of age. In due course that son attained the age of twenty-one years. His father had qualified for the vote, and the son was thereby also qualified and exercised the vote for the past twenty years. Am I correct in interpreting the Act as it stands at present to this effect, that the son is now disfranchised unless he goes before a judge and gets a certificate?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Where was he born?
In Iceland.
Yes, he has to get a certificate.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: I think the son would have to get a certificate.
Then, really this Act is not an enfranchising Act, it is a disfranchising Act.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: No, he has to get a certificate.

But although he has
exercised the vote for twenty years he is disfranchised.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: There may be odd cases of that sort.
They are not odd cases, there are thousands of them.
He was lucky.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Yes.

I am forced to the conclusion that the Government in adhering so rigidly to this unfair clause are simply .seeking to get some political advantage in disfranchising tens of thousands of people who are likely to vote against them, and who by all the rules of fairness are entitled to vote. This can be the only reason, and it will not commend itself to the fair judgment of the country.

Before this matter comes to a vote I would like to say that I agree largely with what the member for Mar-

quette has said. We should consider this amendment seriously before we vote it down, because I am satisfied that it will work some hardship on people in Western Canada-the Icelandic people, and perhaps some people from other countries. In the case cited by the member for Marquette, as I understand it, a young Icelander who had been voting for a number of years would be disfranchised if he did not get a certificate of naturalization. Now, I think that would be unfair; the very fact that citizenship had been extended to the son through the naturalization of the father should entitle the son to the franchise. I am not going to argue that foreigners should be enfranchised simply because they have married British subjects, but I do say that men and women who have lived in Canada for a great number of years and who have already had the privilege of the franchise should not be disfranchised by this Act. I urge upon the Acting Solicitor General and the Government the necessity of carefully inquiring into this question before finally disposing of it. If that is not done, I would ask that the Government make provision for judges to sit at convenient points all over Canada in connection with this matter. This is particularly necessary if the lists to be revised are two years old, as would be the case in some provinces. I am satisfied that if this Bill becomes law in its present form it will work hardship upon hundreds of thousands of people in Western Canada.

I do not quite agree with the principles enunciated, first by my hon. friend the Solicitor General and then by my hon. friend from Algoma (Mr. Nicholson). The elementary right of a British citizen is his right to the franchise. The law of Canada as regards naturalization has been revised on several occasions, and it now is as perfect as it can be. Naturalized British subjects should not be prevented in any way from exercising the franchise, but by this legislation you are putting obstacles in the way of the exercise of the franchise by certain people. The leader of the Opposition has cited instances in which it would be impossible for a woman living in a remote part of Canada to reach a judge in order to get a certificate. It would be more British; it would be much fairer to give de pleno the franchise to the person who has been naturalized. My hon. friend from East Algoma is a stout

Britisher; he will not forget that the question of the franchise has always played a great part in the history of the Empire of which we are all so proud. He will remember that war was declared on South Africa some twenty years ago because the Uitlanders-British subjects- in the Transvaal were denied the right of the franchise by President Kruger, and that on that occasion, a resolution was adopted by this House joining hands with the Mother Country. There is an object lesson for my hon. friends; and if they are true to their ideals,' as I have no doubt they are, they should give the people a fair chance to exercise their right to vote. The hon. member for Algoma has a queer notion as regards female suffrage. He seems to think that by granting woman suffrage we have created a special class of voters. Mr. Chairman, at any election to take place hereafter, there will be no distinction between the female and the male electors; they both belong to one class of citizens-Canadians, exercising their right to vote.

Then if
they are both in the same position why should we not place them in the same position with regard to the securing of the right to the franchise?

That point has already been elucidated. I do not think my hon. friend is putting the question as it should be put before the committee. I am taking exception to the obstacles put in the way of the woman who is a British subject because of her marriage to a British subject. Parliament has granted to that woman the right to the franchise; yet under this proposed legislation, unless she goes a long distance and obtains a certificate you prevent her from reaching the polls. Let us be British; let us be fair; let us be tolerant in the administration of the Elections Act. Remember that it is the elementary right of every British citizen to exercise the franchise. In a country like Canada no such barriers should be put up against the exercise of the franchise.
I think the committee would not make a mistake if they referred this question back to the Committee on Privileges and Elections for reconsideration.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: It would hold up the Bill.

Well,
I still say that it would be worth while to send it back.

When I submitted the
motion which I made I had hoped to appeal to the ordinary sense and fairness of members of the committee. I am still under the impression that the committee is not really seized of the full significance of that which we are debating this afternoon. The hon. member for Algoma East (Mr. Nicholson) gave an extreme case. I am quite in agreement with him that it would not be right and proper, as a general thing, to give the franchise to a woman of any foreign country, who had become a British subject by virtue of, her marriage with a Canadian citizen a few months ago. She comes with him to this country; the hon. member states that under this amendment she would be entitled to vote. That that should be objected to sounds quite reasonable to me. A case like that, however, would not occur in more than one instance out of a thousand, and for my part I would be quite prepared to support some suggestion that would eliminate that sort of thing. If the Acting Solicitor General could bring in an amendment to the Act, whereby women of that class would have to go through the usual period of residence in this country, five years if you like, before they would be entitled to vote, I think he would be on fair ground. The hon. member for Algoma East also stated that he thought these women should be placed on exactly the same basis as the men and go through all the requirements. Very well, then, I will put this question to him:	If men have to
become actually naturalized, to become possessed of naturalization certificates, why has a married woman not the power to obtain the same thing? To-day, under the new Naturalization Act which was passed last session, a married woman has not the power to obtain personal naturalization. That discriminates unfairly against married women. I say that merely by the way, and I think the Naturalization Act should be corrected in that regard.
We have in Waterloo county, as in the West, women of foreign birth who have lived in this country for thirty or forty years, who are Canadians, who have sons who have voted repeatedly in this country, who have daughters who will be permitted to vote. While I do not wish to make any appeal whatever to sentiment-it is, perhaps, made too frequently in this way- it is a fact that, under the law as it exists

now, if this amendment is not accepted, there will be women, who have lived in this country for thirty or forty years and who had sons in the war, who will be put to the necessity of appearing before a judge before they can vote. I want to put this question to every member of the committee, whether a woman of that kind-and I am not exaggerating when I say that there are literally hundreds and thousands of them in this country-is not entitled to at least the same privileges as a woman receives who came here five or six years ago from the United States or from some other North American country. There can be only one reply.
The minister stated a few moments ago that no injustice is done to these men who are obliged to get a certificate, because they have not voted before. I desire to correct him in that regard. The hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) has already referred to the matter. There are meft who came here, as boys with their fathers, from Austria or Germany, whose fathers were naturalized, and under the law as it now stands those men who were permitted to vote even during the war, will no longer be permitted to vote unless the law is changed.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY SIR HENRY DRAYTON, MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
That the Speaker do now leave the Chair for the House to go into Committee of Ways and Means.
He said: Mr. Speaker, following the usual practice I now take advantage of this motion for the purpose of introducing the annual Budget.
The past year has been a difficult and trying one for business practically the world over, and Canada has suffered in common with other nations from the commercial and economic conditions obtaining. The year has been a year of deflation, and deflation is always difficult. Dur-

ing the first portion of the year the price of commodities, instead of declining after the cessation of hostilities, as was generally expected, sharply rose. Extravagant and luxurious buying was common, and the cost of living in Canada unreasonable.
As a corrective measure, as well as for the purposes of revenue, the taxes of last year, commonly known as Luxury Taxes, were imposed. The object of these taxes was stated in the Budget speech as follows:-
Not only is more revenue necessary but extravagant and luxurious expenditure ought to be checked. Just so long as expenditure on nonessentials and extravagant expenditure continues, just so much longer will the drop in the value of essentials be postponed. On those having income more than necessary for properly maintaining themselves and families, there rests a special duty of saving whenever possible and in this manner adding to the available financial resources for development and for industrial undertakings.
Extravagant buying was slowly but surely checked, and in November declines in commodity prices, both manufacturers' and wholesale, were well marked. The buying public which had previously been so well accustomed to rising markets and then bought freely in the fear that prices would be higher, were convinced that the prices of commodities were on the downward trend, and instead of buying in advance of their needs, stopped purchasing as much as possible in the expectation that prices would continue to fall.
But not only were the taxes designed to check wild spending on the part of the public, they were also calculated to cheek unnecessary purchases by the trader, so that his inventories might be all the smaller when the inevitable drop in commodities came, and so that the lower level might be reached, in more easy stages and with little goods on hand.
Having served these main purposes, the so-called Luxury Taxes were, with but trifling exceptions, abolished on the 18th day of December, 1920.
The year has been a trying one in many activities, but it is felt that the lower price levels have been reached, and that working on the sure foundation of lower costs, the conditions of our trade and commerce ought to steadily improve.
Trade
The year just closed gives a great total for Canadian trade. The previous year, notwithstanding that it was a year of rising prices and general activity in business, showed a total of imports and domestic exports of $2,304,008,267, as

against $2,429,288,757 for the year ended March 31, last.
This is a remarkable showing, more particularly in view of the fact that prices had materially declined during the last half of the year and that our heavy export of grain was made on the lower price level. These figures show an increase for the year of $125,280,490. If foreign merchandise brought into Canada r^nd exported be added, the respective totals become for the year ended March 31, 1920, $2,351,174,878, and for the year just closed $2,450,553,175.
For the purpose of comparison, it may be noted that the years at the end of the past two five-year periods, that is for 1916 and 1911, show a total trade of $1,287,117,229 and $741,745,318 respectively. The figures of the past year show great trade activity. Taking nine millions as the approximate population of Canada, and the calendar year as a uniform basis of comparison, it will be found that the aggregate foreign trade per capita in 1920 was $293.30 for Canada, and $127.78 for the United States.
The mere bulk of trade activities does not of necessity, however, show national prosperity. While, on the one hand, the nation may increase in wealth with a comparatively small total business, on the other hand, it is possible to become the poorer in increasing ratio to the amount of gross business done. The vital question is as to whether or not the business as a whole is profitable.
Canada has continued to be a large buyer. Our imports in the year have increased by the sum of $175,608,887, while, on the other hand, our domestic exports have dropped from those of last year by $50,328,397. If the export of foreign produce be included, the total decrease becomes $76,230,590. If mere size of trade was the whole criterion of national prosperity, Canada would indeed be prosperous, and the problems of industrial unemployment and dissatisfaction with farm results entirely non-existent. While it is perfectly true that Canada, relatively, is very much better off at the present moment than many other nations are, the fact nevertheless remains that conditions are not as we would have them.
It has also to be borne in mind that while our total exports are only $76,230,590 short of those of last year, they are $375,741,673 below the gross export peak reached in 1918.
The unfortunate part of our international balances is that with the United States. The unrevised figures for the year show
that our exports to that market amounted to $542,304,456 of domestic, and $18,379,342 of foreign produce, while our imports amounted to $856,593,470, resulting in an unfavourable trade balance between the two countries of $295,909,672. This large unfavourable balance, coupled with the largely increased invisible payments which have to be made to American holders of Canadian securities and investments, of necessity creates a heavy demand for New York exchange, resulting in a premium on New York funds. The real balance against Canada is also increased by the aggregate of the discount on Canadian money in New York, as the trade figures do not include the resultant increased cost to the Canadian purchaser.
If Canada is to continue to buy as much as she now does from the United States, she ought to sell a great deal more in that market. It is undoubtedly to her immediate interest that she should do so. The position of our trade with the United States, unfavourable as it is, is likely however to be made still more unfavourable. The Emergency Tariff, commonly known as the Ypung Bill, which has already been favourably considered by both Houses of the American Congress, calls for the imposition of taxes which would practically prohibit the importation of-in the chief part- Canadian agricultural commodities which amounted in volume during the past year to some $168,350,000. The measure is for but a six months' period, and the permanent Tariff Bill has not yet been brought down.
The legislation is treated as emergency legislation, and is pressed on the ground that the United States have a large surplus of these products, which their farmers are unable to sell, and that the American farmer is subject to unfair competition in the United States market as owing to the discount on Canadian currency the Canadian farmer receives just so many more Canadian dollars, just as useful to him in his own country as the American dollar is to the American farmer.
The underlying difficulty of the whole matter would appear to result from the condition of foreign exchanges and the difficulty of financing overseas sales. Under former conditions, exports of Canadian products, to a large extent, merely added to the exportable surplus of the United States a very profitable business for that country, while to-day, according to statements made in support of the emergency legislation, the stocks of American produce are large, and additions thereto by Cana-

dian imports merely add to the difficulties of the American producer, who cannot today profitably dispose of his own surplus. In other words, what in the past was profitable business for the United States is now regarded as unprofitable.
Our business with the United Kingdom continues to be satisfactory, although it is unaccompanied with favourable balances as great as in the past. Last year our exports to the Mother Country amounted to $495,960,118 while our imports amounted to $126,359,249, resulting in a favourable trade balance of $369,600,869. This year our exports have fallen to $314,226,348, while our imports from the Mother Country have grown to $213,930,946, reducing our favourable trade balance to $100,295,402. In view of the large holdings of Canadian securities in the United Kingdom, while exact figures are not available, the net balance would be much reduced if not indeed turned against us. The showing, however, is very much more satisfactory than that of our trade with the United States and the buyers of English goods have the additional satisfaction of knowing that their dollars were at a premium in the English market.
I have much pleasure in calling the attention of hon. members to the remarkable recovery and extension of British trade in Canada. Imports from the United Kingdom first reached the hundred million mark in 1911. In 1913 they were $138,741,736. As a result of the war, in 1919 the figures had dropped to $73,035,118. In 1920 the total was $126,359,249. The increase of this year over last-although last year's figures were greater than those of any previous year except 1913-is $87,571,697, or over 69 per cent. The sales by the Mother Country in Canada have by the prevailing rates of exchange been made the more easy in the same ratio as our sales to her have been rendered the more difficult. Our sales have also, by reason of the exercise of British Government control, been further restricted.
Revenue, 1920-21
The country's revenues have been well maintained. The revenue for the fiscal year when the accounts are finally closed will approximately reach $432,000,000, as against $349,746,334 for the year before. This marked increase, in a year of deflation, can only be regarded as satisfactory. The chief sources of revenue are as follows:

The estimated expenditure for the year amounts to $533,368,077 as against a total outlay provided by the Estimates of $613,225,411.
The total expenditure has been met without new loans, being covered entirely by current revenue and cash resources available at the close of last year. The amount of cash resources from the past year and applicable to 1921-22 will be relatively small. The figure cannot be definitely stated, as sundry expenditures and revenue for 1920-21 have yet to go through the books. I might say, at this juncture, that we expect to find that the available cash at the end of the year when the accounts are closed will amount to approximately $10,000,000.
In considering the consolidated fund expenditures, having regard to the country's pre-war activities, it will be found that these amount to some $141,000,000. Consolidated fund charges connected with and growing out of the war, such as increased interest, pensions, military records, Air Board, expenses of Land Settlement Board, Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment, etc., and such new services and expenses as cost of collection of war taxation, bonus to the Civil Service, aids granted for technical education and road building, etc., approximate $225,000,000. Debt
As already stated, there have been no fresh borrowings. On the other hand, the debt has increased by the amount that the liquid surplus of the year before has been used, namely, $101,368,077. It should be noted that out of available cash, tax exempt bonds aggregating $89,228,300 have heen acquired and taken off the market. It is proposed to cancel them.
The result is that, having regard to the writting-down of assets which took place last year, the net debt now amounts to $2,350,236,700. An interesting observation may be made as to the increase in debt. In the period 1896 to and including 1914 the net additions to the debt totalled $77,499,417. As compared with this, during the period 1914 to date, if the writing-down of non-active assets had not taken place and if the bare war cost be deducted but resulting current expenses arising from the war such as for interest, pensions, etc, be nevertheless charged, the net debt to-day would stand at approximately $115,000,000 less than at March 31, 1914. The situation may be otherwise expressed by saying that notwithstanding the largely increased cost of Government, to the extent of this sum the country's war activities have been financed out of current revenue.

It is obvious, however, that additional revenues ought to be provided.
Tariff
It is not proposed to put into effect now a general revision of the tariff schedules. While Canada must make her own tariff and while that tariff must be a tariff dictated in the interests of Canada and her people, it is not advisable that frequent changes should be made.
The tariff deals with international business and the proper interests of the

country can only be considered in the light of international business and the tariff laws of other countries. It is idle to attempt to disguise the fact that any proper Canadian tariff must have consideration to the settled tariff conditions obtaining in the United States. Of our total trade of the past year 57 per cent was with the United States. Of total imports of $1,240,125,056, those from our neighbour to the south were $856,593,470 or 69 per cent of the whole.
As already pointed out, temporary tariff legislation of the United States would place a barrier against our exports to that country amounting to no less than $168,000,000. Such or similar action made permanent, of necessity, would require a careful and thorough revision of the Canadian tariff for the purpose of ensuring the proper continuance of Canadian business -of ensuring employment and Canadian stability-a matter of gravest moment to all classes of our citizens, of moment to the farmer as well as to the industrial worker, of moment to the farmer because the home market, always of importance and value to him, would become in view of the action of the United States and of the difficulties of financing overseas sales, more important than ever.
An illustration of the value of the home market under past conditions may be given in connection with the dairy business. The production of butter in Canada for the year 1919 was 226,000,000 pounds and of this amount but 17,000,000 pounds were exported. On the question of profitable prices in the home market, it may be noted that last autumn when the Ottawa wholesaler paid 57 cents for butter and the Ottawa public were paying 59 cents and 60 cents a pound, the export price was 47 cents a pound. The home market is valueless without purchasing power and that purchasing power will diminish or largely disappear with the advance of industrial unemployment. Under the circumstances, having special regard to the fact that there ought not to be a general revision of the Canadian tariff now and another after the close of the United States Congress, no action will now be taken.
In indicating that regard must be had to United States tariff laws when framing the Canadian tariff, I do not desire to be understood as suggesting that the Canadian tariff should, in any way, of necessity follow the American customs rates. The underlying economic principles which apply to tariff necessities of creditor nations, as compared with debtor nations, are entirely different. Creditor nations

are not under the necessity oi. discharging money claims with an excess of visible exports over visible imports or by fresh borrowings. While it is not in the interest of debtor nations to increase money claims against them by an unfavorable balance of visible trade, in the case of the creditor nation it well may be that the only manner in which the creditor nation may receive payment on its investments is by creating money claims in favour of the debtor nation through an excess of visible imports over visible exports.
As a matter of fact, besides goods and commodities creditor nations export coupons, representing interest on borrowed money, while debtor nations import them, that is, pay them. It is impossible to accurately state the amount of coupons annually imported by Canada. In all probability $180,000,000 would not be an outside figure. Under such circumstances, Canada has to be considered as having an adverse balance of $180,000,000 before any consideration is given to the results of her visible import and export trade. On the other hand, a3 a great creditor nation, the United States, apart altogether from her visible imports and exports, has the advantage of a very large invisible export eredit, none the less real because unseen, under the heading of returns from investments. Canada like all other countries in process of development required and indeed still requires foreign capital and is of necessity a debtor nation.
Tariff Changes
Changes in the schedules, however, become necessary for the purpose of implementing the trade pact with the West India Islands which has been ratified by both Houses and assented to. A resolution will be submitted dealing with these.
Amendments to Customs Act
Changes ought to be made in the Customs Act with a view to securing a more efficient carrying out of the principle of the dumping provisions. Much of the unemployment at present existing, results from the importation into Canada of goods at prices below the cost of production. In so far as the public are concerned, little, if any, price advantage has accrued to them through these importations. Indeed, it could not well be expected that they should because these low costs cannot be looked upon as at all permanent and as a matter of fact they have been found to be temporary. It has been established that, after large shipments of
198J
goods have been made from a foreign market and entered at customs at a valuation justified by temporary quotations in that market, prices there have registered substantial increases. The result, however, is directly felt by the Canadian producer and worker. Goods ought to be valued for customs purposes, not at forced-sale prices, justified by temporary quotations to the foreign market, but having regard to the regular standard value in that market and to cost of production and a reasonable profit thereon.
A further change should also be made having regard to the valuation of goods imported from foreign countries whose currencies have greatly depreciated. Under the law, valuations are made in the currency of the country of export and this value has under customs ruling been adjusted to the basis of exchange prices. The increased cost of production in the foreign market does not, however, bear a direct inverse relation to the extent of the depreciation of the currency, more particularly so having regard to countries where currencies are depreciated to a greater extent than 50 per cent. It is therefore proposed to provide that any depreciation of a foreign currency greater than 50 per cent shall be disregarded and that the lowest valuation which can be made will be arrived at by a depreciation of 50 per cent. Where the rate of exchange is adverse to Canada, the value for duty will be computed at the rate of exchange existing at the date of the shipment of the goods. To put into effect these provisions, a Bill will be introduced providing for amendments to the Customs Act as follows:
Section forty of the said Customs Act is amended by adding- thereto the following clause,-"such value in no case to ibe lower than the wholesale price thereof at such time and place," and by adding thereto the following subsection :
(2) Provided that the value for duty of new or unused goods shall in no case be less than the actual cost of production of similar goods at date of shipment direct to Canada, plus a reasonable profit thereon, and the Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue shall be the sole judge of what shall constitute a reasonable profit in the circumstances."
Section fifty-nine of the said Customs Act is amended by adding thereto the following subsection :
(6) Notwithstanding any of the provisions of this section, in computing the value for duty of the currency of an invoice, no reduction shall ibe allowed in excess of fifty per cent of the value of the standard or proclaimed currency of the country from whence the goods are invoiced to Canada, irrespective of the rate of exchange existing between such ooun-

try and Canada on date of the shipment of the goods, and in respect of goods shipped to Canada from a country where the rate of exchange is adverse to Canada, the value for duty of the currency of the invoice shall be computed at the rate of exchange existing between such country and Canada at the date of the shipment of the goods.
Marking of Importations
Representations have from time to time been made to the effect that the goods of one country were being farmed off on the Canadian public as the goods of another country. Especially have representatives of British business urged that many goods were being sold as British goods, which either had not seen Great Britain or were merely collected in and forwarded from that country. In my judgment, immediate effect ought to he given to these representations. Not only has the British importation some right to protection from dishonest competition, but much more so the Canadian public have a right to know from whom they are buying. A resolution will, therefore, be moved to provide that all goods imported into Canada capable of being marked, stamped, branded or labelled without injury shall have indicated on them legibly in English or French the country of origin. This provision will come into force September 1, 1921.
Business Profits War Tax
The Business Profits Tak will be dropped. With present business conditions it would in any event become largely inoperative -excess profits generally speaking will not be found. This tax is one which is only s justifiable as an emergency measure in a time of ascending values and inflation and national stress. It is a tax which works harm to the general financial situation and business conditions in an ordinary period and more particularly in a period of business depression. The Act will not be reenacted.
Excise Taxes
Many complaints have been received from will be abolished. In lieu thereof, having particular regard to the necessities of revenue, duties will be levied on playing cards and wines. The duties on spirits will be increased from the present $3 per gallon customs duty and the $2 additional duty under the luxury taxes, to a straight $10 customs rate. Increase will also be made in the excise duties on spirits of local manufacture released for sale in Canada. The former differential of the excise duty as against the customs duty was 60 cents, a differential of 20 per cent. The excise rate will be increased to $9 a gallon.

Many complaints have been received from hospitals and the producers of proprietary medicines and pharmaceutical preparations who represent that the burden of taxation under the law, which is now being changed and which provides for a total tax of $5 per proof gallon, was unduly heavy. The hospitals in particular represent that they have had great difficulty in properly carrying on. It is proposed to grant a rebate of 99 per cent of the duties paid on spirits actually used for medicinal purposes in bona fide hospitals certified to as such by the Department of Public Health and subject to regulations to be promulgated by the Department of Customs and Inland Revenue for the purpose of ensuring that no abuses take place. Under appropriate regulations it is proposed in the case of patent and proprietary medicines and pharmaceutical preparations to reduce the tax to the rate of $2.40 per proof gallon. This is the rate which applied prior to the enactment of last year's luxury taxes.
Sales Tax
In addition to the foregoing new provisions, it is proposed to increase the rate of the sales tax. Many submissions have been received in favour of a sales or turnover tax. The principle of either a sales or turnover tax has been strongly advocated by many boards of trade and commercial bodies. The general turnover tax in particular has been strongly supported. This tax would call for the payment of a tax on every transaction taking place in the country. It would include
9 p.m. all sales by retailers. Theoretically a general turnover tax on commodities and services has much to commend it. In practical administration, though, in view of the fact that after careful survey it has been established that books are not kept in many retail stores, the cost of administration would be unduly great and difficulties of collection many.
Instead of extending the tax, it is proposed to confine its operation to the sales of manufacturers, wholesalers, jobbers and importers, and to continue a list of special exemptions which, broadly speaking, will cover foodstuffs in their natural state, initial sales of farm produce by the farmer of his own production, as well as the first products of the fisheries, mines and forests.
The 1 per cent and 2 per cent rates on domestic transactions will become 11 per cent and 8 per cent respectively, and the

present import rates will become 2i per cent and 4 per cent. The import rates thus become 1 per cent higher than the like domestic rates. The necessity for this lies in the fact that more than one sales tax is included in the finished article made in Canada, while the materials entering into the manufacture or production of the foreign article are not subject to any such tax.
Mr. Speaker, we in Canada have a great task before us. The world is sadly out of tune. May we help in restoring harmony? Trust and confidence are sadly lacking. Class interests are advanced with selfish insistence. Unemployment is with us. Faith in our fellow-men is weakened. Doubt of 'aie future is often voiced. And what is cne trouoie? The sun still shines-the rivers still sparkle-our lands are as great and fruitful as ever-our resources just as vast. Shall it be said that the work and sacrifice of the past few years were in vain? That we Canadians of to-day do not think that that Canada for whom so great a stream of heroic blood was shed-a Canada great enough to die for-is a country worth living for? Living for Canada! To do that means living for and helping our fellow Canadians, means the realization that no real advantage can be taken by this class at the expense of that-that the wrong of one works to the injury of all-that Canada requires honest, clear thinking and the abandonment of racial, class and political prejudice-that our task is worthy of the efforts of a united Canada and the best, unselfish, constant work of each and all of us. If we can but again renew faith the one in the other
and in our country, live for Canada and in the faith of our forefathers, the future holds no shadows for Canada.

Provided further that when such spirits testing not less than fifty per centum over proof are sold and delivered in such limited quantities as may be prescribed by the Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue to any university or scientific and research laboratory for scientific purposes only, or to any bona fide hospital, certified to be such by the Department of Public Health, for medicinal purposes only, a drawback of ninety-nine per centum of the duty paid may be granted, under regulations to be made by the Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. S. FIELDING (Shelburne and Queen's) :
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we had anticipated that in pursuance of the announcement made some days ago the hon. Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) would have been able to deliver his Budget speech earlier in the day, and that we might then continue the debate at once, but he was kind enough to intimate to me early to-day that, for reasons which he explained, it would be more convenient to him and to the Government to bring on the speech to-night. We then agreed that in that case, after he had delivered his speech, a motion to adjourn the debate would be in order. With that understanding, I desire now to move that the debate be adjourned.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Motion agreed to, and the debate adjourned.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
House again in Committee of Supply, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
Civil Government-Health-salaries, $155,612.50 contingencies, $82,000.
The minister promised us a few days ago a statement regarding the Department of Health.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I might give a very brief review of the work of the department during the year. It will probably be helpful to the committee in considering the Estimates in detail. The Department of Health was created in 1919, and under the Act then passed provision was made for transferring to jthe Department of Health many activities carried on by other departments of the Government, and shortly after the Act was passed, the necessary Orders in Council were put through for that purpose. The quarantine services as well as the work of medical examination that had been previously carried on by the Department of Immigration were transferred. Under some statute in force the Marine Department had been looking after sick mariners. It was thought advisable that that work should also be transferred to the Department of Health, and that accordingly was done. Then the administration of an Act relating to the adulteration of food was transferred from the Department of Agriculture to the Department of Health. There was also some statute relating to drugs, apart from the statute we were discussing the other day, the Opium and Narcotic Drug Act, and its administration was undertaken by the Department of Health. Then there was an Act administered, if I am not mistaken, by the Department of Inland Revenue relating to proporietory and patent medicines. That work also was in due course transferred to the Department of Health. In addition to these old services which were carried on by various departments of the Government, certain new work was undertaken. It will be remembered that when the Act creating the Health Department was before the House, a suggestion was thrown out that it should contain provision for the creation of a branch dealing with child welfare. That branch in due course was created, and is now under the management of Dr. Helen McMurchy, having been in operation for some months. The housing scheme submitted to the Government some two years ago, and finally approved by the Government, was also handed over to the Health Department.
It will be recalled that certain provision was made in the Estimates for dealing with the problem of venereal diseases, the sum of some $200,000 was placed in the Estimates a year ago, and it is proposed to continue the same sum this year, the Department of Health, co-operating with the various provincial departments of

health, with a view to suppressing those diseases as fax as possible. We also had very considerable discussion, I think, at the time the Bill went through, with regard to the advisability of establishing a research bureau in connection with the Department of Health. That has not been done. No progress has been made in that respect, not because a research bureau of the character discussed at that time was not considered advisable, but mainly because we contemplated the establishment of a general scientific bureau at Ottawa, and it was considered wise to let the whole matter rest in abeyance until such time as a decision is finally reached regarding the larger problem.
I do not propose to keep the House very long in dealing with details, but in so far as quarantine is concerned, I may say that the officer in charge of that work for many years in the past, Dr. Montizambert, was retired during the year. He had given long years of service, and, if I remember rightly, he had charge of all our quarantine stations in Canada for something like thirty or thirty-ifive years. During the year, owing to his advanced age, it was thought well that he should be retired, and that some one else should be appointed in his place. Dr. Montizambert gave very long and valuable service to the country in the work he performed during those many years. His place has been taken by Dr. Page, who was formerly our chief medical officer in the Immigration Department at Quebec, and who is now in charge both of the quarantine work and of our immigration medical inspection work. He is now stationed at Ottawa.
We have in Canada four main quarantine stations, one at St. John, one at Halifax, one at Quebec, and one at Victoria. Besides these we have a number of minor stations. Throughout the year, I understand, Dr. Page, the officer mainly responsible for the conduct of these stations, has carefully reviewed the whole situation and has made a number of improvements. Other improvements are very necessary, and that applies particularly to our stations at St. John, Halifax, and Grosse Isle, Quebec; and various sums have been placed in the Estimates for the purpose of providing facilities which are necessary in order that the work of these stations may be properly carried on so as to protect our people from infectious diseases. In addition to actually reviewing the situation at those stations and making provisions for such alterations as were necessary, the Health Department has had two of its
TMr. Calder.]
officers during the past year in Europe and in the United States studying very carefully the plans and methods followed by these countries, and, as a result, I have no doubt at all that a great many improvements will be made in our system in so far as handling these quarantine stations is concerned. Personally, I think, from my own knowledge of the situation and the work carried on during the year, and from the improvements that have already been made, and those that are in sight, I think we may quite confidently say, that there is very little danger of many of the diseases that are now rampant in Europe being introduced into Canada.
As regards the medical inspection of immigrants, I think I may truthfully say that that work is now being carried on much more satisfactorily than was the case in the old days.
