After the discussion we had some two years ago, when the immigration Act was being amended, and on account of the views that were very freely expressed in the House at that time, and the opinions expressed in the press as well, steps were taken to tighten up as far as possible the work that was being done in that respect, and I have no hesitation in saying that the work is now being carried on much more satisfactorily than heretofore. At any rate, I am advised th it fewer complaints reach us in this regard than in the old days.
Two of the officers of the Health Department have also visited Great Britain and Europe for the purpose of advising and helping those who are responsible for passing immigrants at the ports of embarkation. Under the British law, the Board of Trade has its medical officers at the ports of embarkation, and, in addition to that, every shipping company has its medical officers in order to make certain that immigrants that are not sound physically and mentally shall not sail from those ports. Our medical officers have been in consultation with them for some weeks at a time, advising them, as best they can, as to the course that should be followed by them in their inspection and in passing immigrants. I have no doubt whatever that as a result of the work done in that connection very many people have been prevented from coming to Canada who, had they not been rejected at the ports of embarkation, would not have been allowed to land in this country.
We have also adopted the practice during the year of appointing permanent officers for this work. Some five or seven years ago many of our medical inspectors were

merely temporary officers appointed only for short periods, and very often paid by the day. That practice has been entirely abolished and our officers are now permanent men. On the eastern coast, where we have three main ports of entry, namely, St. John, Halifax, and Quebec, in the winter time, when our ports are closed, our officers move to St. John and Halifax, and in the summer, with the great rush of people to Quebec, they locate these. There is sufficient work to keep a full staff of permanent officers engaged, and that plan has been adopted instead of having a number of temporary officers who are changed from year to year. The new plan operates to the advantage of the service generally.
With reference to the care and treatment of sick mariners, it will be remembered that a year ago the fees charged to the owners of vessels were increased, if I mistake not, from one and a half cents to two cents per ton. As a result of the year's operations it will be noted that the fees charged are just a little more than is sufficient to carry on that expenditure- there is a slight saving in that regard. There again, in that branch of our work, the staff has been re-organized. We have adopted the plan of paying our medical officers a lump sum every year for which they are required to render certain services. Heretofore the plan prevailed of paying these men fees for the amount of work which they actually did. Instead of doing so now, we give them a retainer and they are required to give whatever service is necessary in connection with this work; and I am advised that this system is working out very much more satisfactorily than the old plan. We have only some three hospitals left.' I think there were six originally but there are now only three, and it is proposed to close one of those shortly. It is in New Brunswick at a place called Douglastown. Instead of our maintaining hospitals, the plan has been devised of having our sick mariners taken care of in the ordinary hospitals in these seaports for which, of course, we pay the daily rates for the maintenance of the patients.
As regards the administration of the Adulteration of Food Act-

Before the minister leaves
the subject of the Sick Marineer's Fund; do you also pay for the medicines used by the doctors, or do they pay that out of their salaries? -

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I understand the amount paid the doctor covers everything that he is required to furnish in the way of medicines.
He must himself pay for what is required in the shape of medicines. We simply give him a lump sum which is to cover all his expenses in connection with work-his own service plus what medicines he must buy.

Does the minister think
that is a fair proposition? One doctor might have only five patients in the year, and another praetioner might have one hundred and five?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
That is a detail. I would like to have my deputy here when we come to consider details of that nature. At any rate that is the plan that has been devised and, so far as I know, has worked out satisfactorily. In any event no complaint has reached me regarding it.
I made mention of the administration of the Adulteration of Food Act. Under that law Canada has been divided into twenty-five districts, and there again provision has been made for the appointment of permanent officers who will give their entire time to looking after the administration of the law. I am advised that heretofore we had a fairly large staff of part time employees which plan, I understand, has worked out more or less unsatisfactorily. It seems to me that if there is sufficient work to be done under that law it is far better to have a man permanently on the job who is familiar with the law and with its administration. That has been worked out during the past few years, and now we have a permanent staff in some twenty-five districts extending from coast to coast. In addition to that we have laboratories established at Ottawa, Halifax, Montreal, Winnipeg and Vancouver, these institutions existing for the purpose of analyzing the various food commodities where there is any suspicion as to their having been adulterated, and of course a staff of analysts and chemists is employed for that purpose. Last year we had a vote, for this branch of the work of the Health Department, of some $90,000. This year it has been reduced to $80,000, and I dare say, if we had the figures before us for the year, it might have been still further reduced-because I find that the total expenditure for last year down to March 28, was only some $56,000; so it would appear that we will scarcely require the full vote that is asked for this year. As I said, last year $90,000 was asked for; this year we are asking for $80,000; whereas the total expenditure down to March 28, was only some $56,000. It is quite true the books are not closed and that that amount may be

swelled to some extent. The total revenues collected from the administration of the adulteration of the Food Act and the Opium and Narcotic Drug Act amounted to some $38,373.95. Speaking of the Opium and Narcotic Drug Act, I find that there were convictions in 309 cases during the year, and fines were levied totalling some $57,265. Of these fines levied, however, only some $16,697 were collected; in other words, a good many people upon whom fines were levied preferred the jail penalty rather than pay the fine. The amount derived from licenses under the Opium and Narcotic Drug Act was $4,760. I have been given some rather interesting figures to illustrate the effect of the provisions included-I think it was last session- in the Opium and Narcotic Drug Act. I have only the figures for nine months, but I dare say the same figures would be true comparatively for the whole twelve months' period. I find, for example, that during the nine months up to the end of December the total quantity of cocaine imported into Canada was 5,007 ounces as against 2,967 ounces for the same nine months' period of the previous year. In the case of morphine there were 9,838 ounces imported as against 23,666 ounces the previous year; and in the case of gum opium the importations for the nine months period were 2,478 pounds as against 12,837 pounds. Those figures certainly show a very remarkable decrease in the quantities of these drugs imported into Canada for the nine months period ending December 31, last.
I do not know that I should take up the time of the committee just now in relating what ,has been done in connection with housing. I have the figures here, however, and if any member of the committee is interested I shall be very glad to give the moneys that have been allotted each province. I have a statement as to the number of houses that have been built, and as to the manner in which the accounts with the various provinces stand at the present time. If any members of the committee are interested in them. I also have statistics here from all of the provinces, I think, with the exception of one, as to the results of our co-operation with the various health departments in connection with the suppression of venereal diseases. The figures are very interesting. I have some doubt as to whether some of these figures should be given publicity to-that, however, will be a matter for the committee to decide. I have the figures here, and if hon. gentlemen are sufficiently in-
terested in them, and think they should be made public, I will have no objection to submitting them to the committee.

Has
the minister any figures in connection with the mariners' dues, showing the amount collected and the amount expended?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Yes, I have those figures. I made a very brief reference to the creation of the Child Welfare Branch in the department which was created some months ago. We were very fortunate in securing the services of Dr. Helen MacMurchy. Personnally, I feel she is doing splendid work there. She has been co-operating with the various health departments, and as a result of her activities a national body has been created that is very deeply interested in this work. They had a convention last year when some 200 delegates were present, and I understand that another convention will be held this year. I have no hesitation in saying that if the work of that department is carried on for a number of years a very distinct advance will be made by all the provinces in connection with the problem of child welfare.
I have run over only very briefly the main activities of the department. I have numerous statistics before me which I think might well be presented upon the various items of the Estimates when we come to them in detail.

The minister has stated that the quantity of cocaine and morphine imported last year showed a great diminution on the importation of the previous year. This is of course very gratifying news. To what activity in particular does the minister attribute that decrease? Is it through a stricter surveillance? And how far has it been exercised with the medical profession, or the hospitals, or the druggists? It has come to my knowledge during the recess that, regrettable as it may be, some medical men have resorted to selling cocaine and morphine to their patients to satisfy their craving for these drugs. I should like to have some further particulars with regard to the work that has been accomplished in restricting this undesirable trade.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I am inclined to the view that the reduction has come as a result of the change in the law and the close supervision of its administration. In the first place, all importers of these drugs must take out a license; in the second place, local manufacturers of these drugs must

also take out a license; and during the year the department has closely scrutinised the records of these licensees. In addition to that. I think that dealers in these drugs generally have come to recognize the fact that the department means business. The mounted police have been co-operating with the department to the fullest possible extent, and I think the reduction in the illicit traffic is due in very large measure to the knowledge the traffickers have that the mounted police are extremely vigilant. Many of the convictions secured during the year have been the result of the operations of the mounted police. Another factor is that on account of the changes in the law the department has been co-operating to a fuller extent with the local municipal police. In other words, more people have become interested in the proper administration of this law, and I think it is a combination of all these circumstances that has resulted in the figures which I have given to the hon. gentleman.

In so far as the regular importation of cocaine and morphine is concerned, I have no doubt that it is not a difficult matter for the department to get from the importers an exact statement of the different channels through which those drugs have been distributed and as to whether the quantity sold to hospitals, druggists or doctors is more than would be required for their lawful needs. But I understand that a large quantity of these drugs is smuggled into the country, and I doubt very much if the mounted police can accomplish very much in preventing it. However, the department is in a better position to judge than I am. It must be extremely difficult to restrict smuggling entirely.
Now, leaving this subject aside for a moment, I understood the minister to say that the Health Department was represented in the port of New York. Am I correct?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
One of our officers
visited New York.
Has Canada a permanent medical adviser in the port of New York?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No. What I stated was that a couple of our officers had visited Great Britain and the Continent and also the United States to observe the methods there employed in handling quarantine and immigration matters, in order that we might improve our methods if possible.

I have in mind the case of the child of a professor of Laval University who landed in New York with her grandmother and was detained for some time without any apparent reason except that she was not accompanied by her father or her mother. The Minister of Health, who is also Minister of Immigration, will appreciate the predicament in which these two persons found themselves in the port of New York, where they were placed on a small island, I believe, and had to await the arrival of the father of the child, who was notified by wire and arrived on the scene as soon as possible. The department should see that such cases do not occur, especially when the persons concerned are provided with regular passports vised by all the required authorities.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Were these persons held on account of disease, or was the only reason the fact that the child was not accompanied by her parent?

That was the only reason given. I assume that it is a regulation of the American Department of Immigration, but the case could be taken up and looked into. I have no objection to giving my hon. friend the name; the father of the child was Dr. Vallee, whom the minister may know. The child was, I think, with the mother of Dr. Vallee.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: We have at least two immigration officers, not medical officers, at New York. I have no doubt that if that case had been brought to their attention they would at once, if these people were coming to Canada, have advised the United States immigration authorities to pass them along. But it will be understood that on some of these boats thousands of people come in; all sorts of cases have to be dealt with, and the matter may not have been brought to the attention of our officers for some time.

My information is that the case was brought to the attention of the Canadian officer and that he undertook to release the old lady and the granddaughter but was without success for five days, and it was not until Dr. Vallee himself reached New York and showed that he was the father of the child that the child and the grandmother were released.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I shall be glad to look into that case.
Is the old marine hospital in Quebec still used by the Department of Health, and who is in charge of it?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
It has not been in use
recently, but there is a provision in the Public Works Estimates for repairing the old building, and it is to be put in use again. Dr. Nadeau, I understand, will be in charge of the hospital when it is reestablished.

In connection with the
European ports of embarkation, the minister has referred-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Before the discussion proceeds any further I think it is the duty of the Chairman to point out that unless the committee unanimously consents to discuss together all the items of the Department of Health, the Estimates should be considered item by item. I am not blaming the hon. member for Beauce for proceeding to deal with matters of general administration, because he is merely continuing tjie discussion, but if the discussion is continued along the same lines, it will be agreed that all items shall pass together.

Your observation, Mr. Chairman, is warranted, but I am only following the hon. minister in his general review of the work of the department. If I may proceed with the question, I would ask the minister if the department has considered the advisability of having a medical officer at the principal ports of embarkation for emigrants bound for Canada- Liverpool, Rotterdam, Antwerp and Havre. I have brought this matter to the attention of the department in years past with a view to securing on the other side some system of inspection which would reduce or almost entirely do away with the cases of deportation when the immigrants reach this side-[DOT] cases which are very sad indeed in their character. Is the medical inspection at Liverpool, for instance, carried on only by the medical advisers of the ship companies?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
We have had a couple
of officers over there during the last six months, more for the purpose of advising the local authorities-that is, the Board of Trade doctors and the shipping doctors. We discussed this matter on the Immigration Estimates; evidently the hon. member was not present at the time. No one would be more pleased than I would be if we could arrange just what the hon. member suggests. Under ordinary conditions, in order to accomplish the object to which my hon. friend refers, it would be necessary to have a staff on the other side to examine medically all persons coming to Canada and give them a certificate which would enable them to land in Canada, taking the respon-

sibility entirely off the shoulders of the transportation companies. In other words, we would have to maintain a staff on the continent sufficient to look into the cases of all persons desiring to come to Canada, not only from the standpoint of health, but from the standpoint of mentality as well. Now, it would not be sufficient to do that in respect of the people who left Liverpool for Canada, because many persons leave other ports to come to this country-Bristol, London, Southampton, Queenstown, Belfast, Glasgow, and so on. The great bulk of the people may come through certain ports, yet some come from all these other ports. Take the continent:	the
Italians, for instance, come from Genoa; the Greeks come from ports in Greece, and the same is true all the way around. If you are going to amend a law of this kind so that it will be applicable to all people, the only thing to do is to establish special machinery to handle the whole population in every country in Europe. As I explained to the committee the other day, I estimate that it would cost two or three or probably four hundred thousand dollars, simply to place at the different ports ordinary medical practitioners who could discover a contagious disease such as measles or smallpox or something of that kind. You would also have to have your mental experts. Supposing a man wants to leave Roumania or Greece for Canada and there 10 p.m. is a question as to his mental condition. Where are we to catch him?-in Roumania or Greece or at one of our ports? The same problem may come up in the case of a man in the north of Scotland. He leaves from Glasgow. Are we going to put in a special staff so as to catch such a man at that port? The same thing is true as regards all other ports throughout Europe. There is no doubt that the system suggested by the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Beland), if it were not for the enormous expense involved, is the proper system, but it would involve the expenditure of a very large 'ted to develop that system in Great Britain, sum of money. The United States attempted to develop that system in Great Britain, but after trying to operate it for some time they had simply to abandon it. We throw upon the transportation company the responsibility of deciding whether an intending immigrant ip all right from the health and mental standpoints. They have their medical officers, and we place large penalties upon the transportation companies if they make a mistake. In

addition to that, the British Board of Trade are interested in the examination of every emigrant who leaves the British Isles, and they have their medfieal officers at all British ports in order to safegard their people who wish to go to Canada and other countries. They have a system of supervision, so that you have the double check-[DOT] the Board of Trade and the medical men of the transportation companies.
Last year for a period of some six months we sent overseas two of our medical men who are thoroughly acquainted with our requirements, standards and,1 everything of that kind. They have got in touch with the medical men of the British Board of Trade and the shipping companies, both in Great Britain and on the continent, at the chief ports. As a result of their representations and work, very much of the hardship that had been occurring in the p^st has been eliminated. Instead of attempting to establish machinery overseas under which certificates will be given to people giving them the right to land. I rather think it will be better from our standpoint to extend our work there so that we shall have a supervising staff to aid these people in clearly understanding our law and its operation. As the matter stands now, we have the whole problem on the east coast of Canada centralized at the three ports of St. John, Halifax and Quebec, and we can keep at those three points a comparatively small staff of thoroughly trained men, men who work at that class of work for. months and months at a time and get very expert at it so that they can have a pretty clear idea, simply by looking at a person, whether or not he should be set aside for examination. To train a large staff to carry on that work properly and to be spread over a large part of Europe would cost a great deal of money.

I have not suggested in particular that the minister and his department should undertake to inspect on the other side of the sea would-be immigrants to Canada. I only asked the minister whether he had considered the advisability of doing that. I realize the force of his argument that the expenditure would be very heavy and if cases of deportation are not numerous, I do not see the advisability of resorting to that policy at all. The minister is, perhaps, in a position to tell the committee what number of deportations' occurred during last year.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Those figures were given when we were on the Immigration Estimates.
Leaving that aside for the moment, may I ask the minister whom the department sent abroad to inspect the different ports and confer with medical officers of the different transportation companies?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Dr. Nadeau was in
Europe for a period of about five months. When he returned we sent over Dr. Jeffs. Dr. Jeffs has now been overseas for about three months. We have really covered a period of eight months instead of six months as I mentioned.

I understand that Dr. Nadeau visited the principal ports of Continental Europe. I have known Dr. Nadeau for a great number of years, and no better qualified man could have been selected to make the tour, confer with medical men connected with the different ports and give them advice regarding our regulations. Why was the other doctor sent over? Was he sent over to complete this mission or was he sent on another mission?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The department has
adopted the practice of using every endeavour to train its chief officers. Dr. Nadeau was sent across in order that he might familiarize himself with the situation in Great Britain and Europe. He spent some five months there for that purpose, and I am sure the hon. member can understand that, in addition to his giving advice, he would also learn a good deal that would be very valuable to him on this side. When Dr. Nadeau returned, he went down to New York, and it was thought well to send over one of our other doctors interested in this work. This scheme of sending our medical officers across the seas is part of the general scheme of the department of' giving our chief officers every opportunity for a thorough training in the work of the department.
Who has replaced Dr. Page who, I understand, has been promoted to the position formerly occupied by Dr. Montizambert?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Dr. Nadeau of Quebec.
He is in charge of the Immigration hospital?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
He has charge of the
medical end of our work there. Dr. Page was immigration agent and medical

speakerposition: subtopic
stagedirection
speechtext: inspector at Quebec. I think Mr. O'Connor is now the agent at Quebec and Dr. Nadeau is health officer at Quebec.

Dr. Montizambert has
been a very long time with the department as a higher health officer and later, I think, as General Superintendent of Quarantine Stations in Canada. The minister stated that Dr. Montizambert had been superannuated. Was he retired under the provisions of the Civil Service Act passed last session?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: He was under the old superannuation law, and was retired under its provisions.
At his own request?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No, I could hardly say that. I think he was quite prepared to carry on.
We are all sorry to lose Dr. Montizambert's services, and our sorrow is only diminished by the fact that he has been replaced by such a distinguished medical authority as Dr. Page.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: He is a first-class officer.
The very best.
The department is now administering the Opium and Drug Act. How many convictions have been secured, and what quantity of these drugs has been seized?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
There were some 309
convictions. I have not the information before me as to the quantity of drugs seized. In the case of these 309 convictions, there were fines imposed to the amount of $57,265. These fines were not all collected, as some of those convicted preferred to stay a while in jail. The amount actually collected in fines was somewhere in the neighbourhood of $16,000.

-What I am trying to get at is the amount of these drugs that were attempted to be brought into Canada through illegitimate channels. It is quite easy to keep track of what comes in legitimately, but I do not think we are warranted in saying there are certain reductions. unless we have some evidence to that effect. All that we know is that there has been a reduction through legitimate channels.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That is quite correct.

I would like to ask the minister-I brought this question up when the Bill creating the

department went through the House a couple of years ago-if there is not some way of making this Act self-sustaining. Can we not make the fees sufficiently high to pay for the administration of the Act?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: To a certain extent the Act is self-sustaining. Let me give an example. The Department of Health deals with the Act respecting the adulteration of foods and the Opium and Narcotic Drug Act. We also have been administering Acts respecting feeding suffs and fertilizers, proprietary and patent medicines, and marine hospitals. In the case of these services the expenditures for last year down to March 28, amounted to $128,382.77, and the revenue derived from the administration of these laws amounted to $126,934.36. That shows a deficit in so far as these services are concerned, of only $1,448. Of course, there are other services. You will find in the general vote, an item for quarantine, for example, in the neighbourhood of $250,000. You could not make that service self-sustaining. Then you have the Civil Government vote of $231,537.

When may we expect to have a scientific branch started? Along with the hon. member for South Toronto (Mr. Sheard) I impressed the necessity of this upon the House when the Bill was going through, and when I left the chamber in the old museum I was very much astonished by what a Cabinet minister who has since given up that rank told me. He said that t had only been advocating the passing of an Act which would simply be used for creating more positions and voting more salaries, and that the Act would be absolutely useless. It rather surprised me that a man whom we would have expected to have better judgment could make such a statement. I do think that if this department is going to have any justification for its permanent existence, we ought to branch out into the scientific line. All these other Acts have been successfully administered, perhaps just as successfully as now, by other departments, and I do think that if Canada is going to take her place among the nations of the world in a scientific sense, and if the Department of Health is going to play the part it should play, it is absolutely essential that a scientific branch should he established, with a man in charge with the proper scientific attainments and qualifications. It seems ridiculous to me to see in the Estimates an item

of $10,000 for research, and $200,000 for veneral diseases. It is almost a travesty on our intelligence to bring before Parliament items of that kind. Can the minister hold out any hope of having this department put on a real scientific basis in the near future.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: All I can state at present is that the Estimates contain a sum of $10,000 for research work. I am not in a position to state what the further policy of the Government may be in this regard. I may, however, throw this out as a hint as to what may happen. I stated at the outset, when dealing with the Estimates generally, that there is a possibility that provision may be made for a research laboratory somewhere in Canada. In my judgment it would be very foolish to establish a separate laboratory for our purposes. If we are going to have a general scientific laboratory for carrying on scientific, research and investigational work, it seems to me that whatever we require in that direction should find a place in that laboratory in order to save expense and duplication, but until that larger question of policy is determined I am not in a position to state anything further in regard to the matter.	,

I do not
agree that that is the larger question of policy; I think it is the minor one. The question of industrial or scientific research is an entirely different matter. We have also been advocating that in this House for a good many years, and I am glad that the Government have at last passed a Bill for that purpose. As far as a home for a scientific department is concerned, it might be housed in the same building as the Department of Health, but I do not see how one could be brought under the other or even associated with it. The objects are quite different; scientific and industrial research is ah entirely different thing.

I did
not get the information I asked for with regard to sick mariners.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I was just wondering
whether we were going to take up the items separately. I shall be very glad to give the figures when we come to that item.

I
understood that we were going to consider the items together until we got our information.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think the committee have agreed to that, and that all the items are to be passed together the moment the discussion concludes.
That is the way I understand the matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That is quite agreeable to me. The hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair), wanted to know the revenue derived from marine hospitals. The fees collected in 1919-20, the full year, amounted to $78,227.04, and the expenditure amounted to $88,886.36. For the year 1920-21, down to March 28, just prior to the close of the year,-these figures will not be absolutely accurate because the books were not closed at that time-the department had collected $79,047.25, whereas the expenditure down to that time, March 28 this year, amounted to $69,286.97. In other words, there was about $10,000 on the credit side of the ledger.
That is very satisfactory, but I understood that the rate was increased to twice what it was before. Is that correct?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No, it was increased from one and a half cents to two cents.

The
rate has been doubled.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No; if it were doubled, it would be three cents.

Is it
not three cents now?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No, two cents.

Then I think there should be a larger increase in the revenue. The revenue in 1919, under the old rate, was $69,243.65, according to the returns, so that there is very little increase in the revenue this year.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I understand that the new rate only went into effect on January 1 of this year, so that there will be nine months of the last fiscal year under the old rate.

Do
government ships pay dues the same as other ships? We have two classes of government ships, the ordinary marine vessels that are used for lighthouse service, like the Stanley and the Lady Laurier, and ships of the Canadian Government Mercantile Marine. Do both or either of these classes of ships pay the ordinary dues?
313G

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I understand that the government ships have not been charged this rate.
None of them?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
No, the reason being
that in the past none of the government ships run by the Customs Department, the Inland Revenue Department, or the Marine Department, have ever paid these fees. Where their mariners have been sick they have been taken care of in the ordinary way, and the accounts for their care have been charged against the department. That is the custom that has prevailed in the past.

That
does not seem to be fair.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I do not like it myself.	.

There
is no reason in the world why Government ships should escape taxation and the care of the mariners employed by the Government should be thrown on the other ships. But that is apparently what the Government does. I notice by the Auditor General's report that this statement is borne out, a considerable sum of money having been expended in taking care of sailors on Government ships. Apparently this expenditure is charged against the revenue collected from the ordinary mercantile ships. This seems to me to be a grievous discrimination. The Government has never taken care of sick sailors on the coast of Canada; I can make that statement without the slightest hesitation. They have neglected the duty of looking after these sick mariners, and I know this to be the case in my own constituency as well as along the coast of Nova Scotia. Every hon. gentleman in this House from that part of the Dominion knows that proper attention has never been given by the Marine Depart-n>ent to sick sailors in Eastern Canada. The way in which doctors are paid is a good illustration of the Government's policy. The doctor is given a lump sum of $400 or $500, and he is supposed to provide medicine out of that. You can understand what this means in a port where sick sailors come in requiring expensive medicine. It simply means that the sailors do not get medicine at all, for it would be impossible for the doctor to buy drugs, at present rates, to be prescribed for any number of sick sailors out of the small amount he gets as a salary. That is one of the systems carried on by the Government in the
 -
penurious way in which they have dealt with this matter. I protest against the practice of charging the care of sick sailors on Government ships against this fund, as well as against the neglect which is shown these men, the reason for which is the alleged fact that there is no money in the fund to look after them. As a matter of fact, there has been a considerable surplus in this fund for a good number of years. I remember that this matter was looked into some time ago, and there was a large sum of money-some $200,000 I believe-of a balance to the credit of the fund. Application was made in my own constituency many years ago for some accommodation for the sick sailors at the town of Canso, which is the largest fishing port in the Dominion, or at all events, on the Atlantic coast. More ships call there and more sailors visit that port than is the case with any other port in Eastern Canada; and yet there is no accommodation for sick sailors. The nearest marine hospital situated at Louisburg, which is 140 miles distant from Canso by any means of public conveyance. No steamer runs between Canso and Louisburg, and the only way of reaching the latter place from Canso would be to take the patient up to Mulgrave, some thirty miles away, and then to Sidney, another ninety miles and from thence to Louisburg or to Anti-gonish, which is also a long distance from Canso. The only thing to be done in a case like this is to provide some hospital accomodation at Canso itself for sick sailors. This question has been brought to the attention of the department many times, but nothing whatever has been done. I presume that the ships of the Mercantile Marine are treated in the same way, are they not? Do they pay?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
When the hon. member
asked his question, he referred to Government ships, and I immediately asked the officers if they paid the ordinary tonnage rate and was advised that they did not. But they had in mind, not the Canadian Merchant Marine, but the ordinary boats run by the different departments, which do not pay. The Canadian Merchant Marine boats pay the same as the others. With reference to doctors engaged at comparatively small figures running from $300 to $400, in the great majority of cases the sick seamen are sent to hospitals and the charges for medicines and supplies are included in the hospital bill.

But
take a place where there is no hospital?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Where that does not prevail, the medical man himself out of the annual fee agreed upon provides whatever is required in the way of medicine. He is a party to the agreement, he expects it, that is his bargain, it is understood; so there cannot be any very great hardship in that connection. After correspondence and consultation with these men they came to an agreement as to what amount should be charged as an annual fee.

It is
news to me that the doctor is allowed to state the amount he will take for attending the sailors and paying for the medicine. If that was the case there would be no complaint, and we would not have cases like that at Canso where a small sum of about $500 is paid to a doctor, which amount is to include the cost of medicine. My hon. friend's statement is not really a recital of what actually does happen. The doctor is offered a small sum to attend to this duty at the port, but he is not consulted as to what medicine shall be used. If he were he would tell a very different story from that told by my hon. friend. It is a cause of complaint among the doctors all along the coast that, out of the small salary they receive, they have to furnish medicine principally to the sailors. It is an improper method in the first place and my hon. friend ought to correct it. There should be a separate account for the medicine. The medicine is one thing; the doctor's service is another thing. They should not be mixed up together in the way my hon. friend states because it operates to the neglect of the sailor; it cannot operate otherwise. Sometimes expensive medicine is required, the [DOT] salary of the doctor is often not more than $400 or $500, and it would be impossible, as every medical man knows, to give any decent treatment on a salary like that and pay for the medicine, especially as the sailor is a long time under the doctor's care. The system is wrong, and I would like my hon. friend to say now, before we get through with this discussion that he will correct it. This matter has been turned over to the Department of Health. The Marine Department is not supposed to know anything about health matters, but this department does know, it is their business, and they ought to deal with the question in a businesslike way. Pay the doctor a certain salary for looking after the sailors, and pay for whatever medicine is required out of the fund. The fund is in a healthy condition so far, and there is no reason why
we should be penurious about it. It has given a credit balance this' year, it will likely give a larger one next year. It has constantly given a credit balance, I think, and there is a large balance to the credit of the fund when you add up the results of the different years. Now, there is no reason why we should treat sailors this way. We are collecting money from the ships for the special purpose of taking care of them, and the Government is a trustee for the distribution of that money. I want to be emphatic on this question; the matter should be adjusted by the Health Department and adjusted at once.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I am inclined to agree
with the statements made by the hon. gentleman who has just spoken. The matter has now come to my attention and I can see that there is a good deal in the argument. I might state, however, that the amount that has been fixed for a fee for the doctor at these various ports has been based upon past experience covering a number of years. Well, that in itself may be all right, but I can quite conceive of a case where a doctor might have half a dozen sick mariners, with a certain class of disease, or diseases, that would require a great deal of costly medicine. I can quite conceive of that, and it seems to me that the suggestion thrown out is worthy of every consideration and should be gone into with a view of seeing whether or not we cannot work out a system along the lines which have been suggested. I can promise the hon. gentleman that I will be only too glad to do that. I will admit at the same time that I can see a great deal of force in his argument, and I hope we will be able to work out some plan along that line.

Will
my hon. friend also look into this question of the hospital at Canso?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I will be only too glad
to do so.
I would like him to give that matter serious attention.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I shall look into it.

1
would like my hon. friend to do this specially because I know it is the policy of the Government to close up these hospitals, and it is a good policy in places where ordinary hospitals exist for treatment.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: What is the nearest hospital to Canso?
I was explaining to my hon. friend that there were two or three hospitals, but I suppose the hospital in Antigonish would be the nearest.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: About how many miles distant would that be?

About
a hundred. It is rather difficult to remove the patient, who is on a boat, to the train and convey him to the hospital at either Antigonish, Louisburg, or Halifax; there are three hospitals to which patients from Canso can be sent. Men have lost their lives at Canso in recent years because they could get no proper treatment there. In some cases it was impossible to remove them to'a hospital, they had to be treated in a kitchen or some place where people would take them in, as there is no hospital of any kind there. The consequence has been that sailors have not had the proper treatment at that place. The matter has been brought to the attention of the Marine Department constantly for years back, and promises have been made but nothing has ever been done. I would submit that the proper way to deal with this question would be to have a cottage hospital at Canso, and for the department to agree to pay a substantial sum for the purpose of maintaining it, throwing the rest of the burden upon the town. There is no reason why something should not be done by the town as well as by the Government provided the hospital can be made to serve the sick of the town as well as the sailors. I think an arrangement could be made by which the local people would bear part of the burden, if the Government would give a substantial amount each year towards maintaining a small hospital there to look after these sick mariners.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I shall be very glad to look into it.

My hon. friend from Guysborough has been very moderate in his figures. The fact of the matter is that these medical men are often only paid $300, and the medical man in his own town of Canso was only paid $468.75 for fifteen months' work.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: He will get $550 next year.

Well, if he got $550, as my hon. friend has said, he would expend that in drugs if he gave proper treatment to the patients. The same condition

obtains all along the coast. My hon. friend has made a strong plea for a hospital at Canso. He has made out a very strong case, I admit, but the same condition obtains along other sea-coasts. Take the coast of Inverness county. There you find one hundred miles of sea-coast where a large percentage of the population devote their entire time in the summer season to fishing and sailing. These men go outside the province, and therefore are entitled to participate in the Sick Mariners' Fund. There is not a hospital within a hundred and fifty miles, there is no hospital in the county, I may say, but an effort is now being put forth to build a hospital there. I would suggest to the minister that perhaps he could adopt some policy or other by which the department would give reasonable assistance to the building of that hospital. The department would then have, so to speak, a claim on that hospital for the treatment of the sick mariners. I would urge him to take that matter into consideration. As to the salary paid to the doctors, the policy now adopted is simply unique. I can explain it because those concerned are doctors, and as usual they give their services for nothing. I could tell my hon. friend the number of patients that have been treated in Cheticamp, but before doing that I would ask the minister one question: Do these men send in any report to the department as to the work they do, or as to the number of patients they treat? I see my hon. friend has the data there. If I were to tell the minister the number of patients that have been attended to at Cheticamp and Grand Etang alone, he would be surprised and would wonder how the doctors could have given those patients" proper attendance and medicines on the small amount of money that is allotted. So really I am afraid the doctors accept these positions simply because their work is humanitarian. The minister's explanation a moment ago is not sufficient. It is not fair to say that because these men have been generous enough to give their work for nothing, merely getting sufficient from the Government to pay for the drugs they prescribe, that the present inadequate remuneration should be continued. It is not encouraging. These men, I suppose, would give much better service if it were shown that the country appreciated their work, and the only practical way of showing that appreciation is by the Government increasing the salaries, and that is a most reasonable request. I think the department should

come to one conclusion, and that is to pay these men something reasonable or tell them, "We do not want your services."

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Probably it I had before me a statement of the number of patients each officer treated in the year I would be able to give some justification for the method that has been followed. But I quite realize the force of the argument presented by the hon. gentleman. It is quite possible that a doctor might spend all his remuneration on drugs if he is doing the right thing by his patients. I shall be quite prepared to go into the whole subject sympathetically with a view to trying to meet the arguments that have been advanced.

I am very glad indeed that . my question has brought forth this discussion, because the subject is a very important one and affects certain officials of his department in the maritime provinces. It was brought to my attention some years ago that the physician who was looking after the marine hospital in my home town was not receiving very much for his services. I think if the minister will look over his statistics he will find that more patients are treated in the marine hospital at Lunenburg than in any other hispital on the Atlantic coast. This man, although to-day getting $500, which includes the medicines he has to purchase for the sick mariners he attends, only two years ago was getting but $300.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: $600 this year.

But he got only $500 last
year.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes.

He is a very worthy
physician and gives excellent care and attention to his patients. I feel confident that if the minister will look into the matter he will come to one conclusion, that the payments for salary and medicine should be separate. During the war when medicine was very expensive this doctor informed me that it took practically all his salary to pay for the medicines he supplied. The hospital is about two miles from the town and he has to drive out there three or four times a day to look after the patients as well as to go aboard the ships and examine the sick mariners before they are taken to the hospital. The position is no sinecure and the doctor should be paid a good fair salary.
I agree with what the hon. member for Guysborough has said in regard to the
Canso hospital. Vessels from my county call at Canso perhaps more than at any other port in Nova Scotia or Newfoundland. It is a port of call for these vessels when going either to the Grand Banks, the banks off Nova Scotia coast, or up into the gulf of St. Lawrence. I have seen in the port of Canso 100 sail of vessels carrying crews of from fifteen to twenty men. There is no hospital there at the present time, and one should be established at the earliest possible moment, for the reason that sick mariners landed at Canso to-day have in a great many cases first of all to be taken from their ship to another ship which runs from Canso to Mulgrave and then transferred to the train for Halifax. I have known of several cases where sick men landed from ships belonging to my own county have died on the way to Halifax, and in other cases their condition has been so imperilled that their lives were despaired of for a long time. This condition of affairs should be remedied at the earliest possible moment.
Another matter which should be attended to is the treatment of sick mariners who are landed at Newfoundland ports. As the minister is well aware, 150 sail of vessels carrying some 3,000 men leave the county of Lunenburg every June on what is known as the summer fishing trip and proceed to the Grand Banks, about 100 miles east of Cape Race. While on the banks they call at Cape Broyle, St. Johns, Carbonear, Burin and other Newfoundland ports and land any sick men, but under the Act there is no provision for looking after them when tjhey are sent home to Nova Scotia. That is to say, they are not allowed to enter their home hospital for the simple reason that they were taken sick outside the province, and consequently the owner of the vessel has to pay for the men's passage home and then the men themselves or their employers have to pay for their medical attendance and hospital bills. I think the minister will agree with me that the ' department ought to pay these expenses, or allow the men to enter hospital immediately on their return to their home port. The present situation is very unfair in view of the fact that these ship owners pay their fees and are getting no benefit therefrom. I trust the minister will look into the matter and issue orders that under these circumstances the men shall be properly looked after by the Health Department.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I shall be very glad to look into that question as well. In the

case of these fishing vessels, if a man is seriously ill and landed in Newfoundland, is any provision made for caring for him there?
None whatever; the owners of the vessel have to pay all the bills.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: And if a man is capable of being moved he is taken back to Nova Scotia and the owner of the vessel must pay his fare and all expenses until such time as he is placed by the department in some hospital.

No, the man comes home; he has to pay his own doctor's bills and get his own medicine, or the cost is met by the owners of the vessel. The department will take no responsibility and will not pay the bills.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I shall be very glad tc look into it.
I would like the minister also to look after the Minister of Marine and see that he pays his sick mariners' bills as well as other people.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Is my hon. friend referring to the Canadian Merchant Marine?

I am referring to the ordinary vessels in the Government service such as the Laurier and the Stanley and the Montcalm and a number of others, all with large crews. The care of these men, when ill, is all charged up against sick mariners' dues, and nothing is paid into the fund by these, Government vessels. I find, however, in the Auditor General's report that expenditure is charged up against this fund.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It is recouped by the department. In the first instance it is charged up against the fund but the accounts are finally squared by calling upon the department to reimburse the amount.

Well, the expenditure is here, making up the amount that my hon. friend said he had spent during the year. The vessels are the Aranmore, Druid, Estevan, Lady Laurier, Laurentian, Light Ship 15, Montcalm, Stanley, Tug Lisgar, Patrol Boat Bethelama, Patrol Boat F, Lillooet and Madras. These boats are mentioned in the Auditor General's report and expenditures made in connection with them are all apparently added into the expenditure that my hon. friend has mentioned.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My hon. friend will find a corresponding amount on the revenue side.

I submit I am entitled to an explanation from my hon. friend. I have already understood him to say that no money was collected from the sailors on these Government vessels. Now, here is money expended from the fund, and that is what I want explained.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: As I have already stated, if there is a charge of this kind for taking care of sick mariners on these vessels the charge is first made against this fund and afterwards the amount which is paid is reimbursed by the department owning or operating the vessels.

Why'
is that not shown in the Auditor General's report?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It will be found on the revenue side.

When my hon. friend looks into the matter which I mentioned with regard to sick seamen, will he advise me when he has the information, because in a month's time the vessels will be leaving for Newfoundland, and I would like to be able to advise the captains as to the position they will be in.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I shall be very glad to do that.

I have on several occasions directed the attention of my hon. friend's department and of the Marine Department to a most peculiar condition which exists: a vessel sailing between ports in Nova Scotia cannot participate in the sick mariners' fund, but if that vessel goes to Magdalen Islands or any place outside the province, she may participate in the fund. That has always struck me as a most extraordinary condition.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The law would have to be amended to change that.

That is what I have been protesting against all along. For the last fourteen years I have been bringing the matter to the attention of the Minister of Marine, because it does pot appeal to me as being reasonable.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It does not strike me as reasonable.

Will the minister
give me the promise that he will look into the matter and that he will bring do-'*-*-

legislation next year removing that absurdity?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I will not promise to
bring down legislation, but offhand it strikes me as a very peculiar arrangement. You have the condition where a boat which makes a small trip of ten miles outside the province-say, to an adjoining province-comes under the operation of the law, whereas, if the trip is, say, 400 miles around the coast of the province, the law does not operate. It seems to me that there must be some history in connection with this law when it has stood for fourteen years notwithstanding frequent protest by hon. members. I shall certainly . look into the matter and see what the explanation of it is.
If there is any history I have never been able to learn it; I never could get any explanation from the minister or from the officers of the department.

I can give the minister
another thought with regard to the way this matter works out. A vessel leaving a port in Nova Scotia to proceed to another port in Nova Scotia to load for a foreign port does not come under the operation of the Act. For instance, two years ago, during the influenza epidemic a number of vessels were chartered in Nova Scotia to go to North Sydney and load coal for St. John's, Newfoundland, and then to proceed to Barbados or Europe. When they arrived at North Sydney the crews took sick. These vesesls had paid sick mariners' dues but it was found under the Act that the crews could not be received in the hospital and that the Marine Department, under whose charge the sick mariners' dues were at the time, would take no responsibility. The result was that although, as I say, the vessels had paid their sick mariners' dues, the owners of the ships-or the sailors themselves, whether they went home or were under the doctor's care in North Sydney-were compelled to pay their own expenses. I tried to get the Minister of Marine to change the law a year ago but nothing has been done. I certainly think that the crews of vessels which have to proceed to a local port to take cargo to a foreign port should, in case of illness at the port where the vessel is loading, be treated in the same manner as if tie illness had taken place in other than a local port.

There is a good deal of misrepresentation on the part of dealers and manufacturers with regard to the supplying of coffee to the consuming public. There are offered for sale in tins different brands of coffee, all more or less represented as the pure article and as more delicious than the coffee you would obtain if you ground the beans yourself. Now, is the department taking any action in this regard? I know of some ground coffee retailing at 70 or 75 cents a pound in which there is not more than 25 per cent of real coffee the remainder being made up of peas, chestnuts, acorns, tree leaves and so on. It is one of the greatest exploitations of the public by unscrupulous dealers. Will the department not take the matter in hand, gather samples of the different brands of coffee that are offered for sale in tins, analyse them and put through regulations, or, if the department has no authority, have legislation passed to compel those manufacturers to specify clearly on the tins: "This contains 20 per cent of coffee only and no more"? The public is under the impression that it is getting the pure article, or at least 75 per cent coffee and, say 25 per cent chicory. A mixture like that is a good one and a very agreeable beverage, but will you find a single one of those mixtures containing more than, say 30 per cent of coffee? I do not believe you will. The department seem to be absolutely heedless of this shameful exploitation of the consuming public. I am a drinker of coffee, and I always ask myself why the department does not take up this question. My answer is that the officials are Englishmen who are used to tea, and they do not care about the quality of the coffee. But try to make an old English lady drink adulterated tea, a tea that is only 20 per cent pure, and you will hear a storm brewing somewhere.
"A tempest in a teapot."

It will be "a tempest in a teapot" this time. As regards coffee, which is a wholesome stimulant, which is an article that you will find on every breakfast table in Quebec and very much now throughout the English provinces, why should we not be supplied with the pure article or, at least, know what we are getting? We do not know. This commodity is being sold at a fancy price without the public having any possibility of knowing whether the product is adulterated or not.
To pass from coffee to maple products, according to the existing law you are sup-

posed to get only the pure article when you buy maple sugar, or maple syrup especially. I make the statement without any fear of successful contradiction that the market is flooded with adulterated maple syrup. Unscrupulous manufacturers and dealers now avail themselves of the general impression that prevails that when you see maple syrup on a tin, it must be and is pure; but in the majority of cases it is not the pure article; it is a mixture, and the public should know that it is a mixture and the exact quantity of pure maple syrup which the article contains should be stated. I insist upon the department collecting samples, not only of maple syrup, but especially of ground coffee offered for sale in tins and letting the public know what they contain. These articles will then sell at the price at which they should be sold, and that is a few cents a pound and no more.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I am personally glad the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Beland) has brought these matters to our attention. Canada, as regards the Adulteration of Foods Act, is now divided, as I stated at the outset, into five districts. During the year we have adopted the policy of having permanent officials in charge of the work in each of those districts. I find, for example, that in Montreal we have four officers, one of whom is on part time. There are a few part-time officers still left. We throw the administration of the law upon these permanent officers; it is their duty, under the law and under instructions from the department, to endeavour, in every way possible, to chase up people who deal in these adulterated food products.
I am afraid the officers are too lenient as regards coffee especially.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I am very glad the hon.
gentleman has called our attention to the matter because it will be my business to take it up with the department as regards these two products, at least; that is maple products and coffee. The hon. gentleman rather frightens me because I use daily one of these coffees put up in a tin can.
The minister is drinking peas all right.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I had better have it
analysed just for the purpose of knowing what I am drinking daily because there may be but a small proportion of pure coffee in the article. There is no doubt that if either of these conditions prevail, if the market is

being flooded with large quantities of coffee that is not coffee at all or that contains only a small proportion of pure coffee, we and the public should know that. If we have a law that provides for the sale of pure maple products, and if that law is not being lived up to, we should follow the matter up, and see that the law is carried out.

Have all the provinces
availed themselves of the amount that was voted last year for combatting venereal
diseases?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
All of the provinces,
with the exception of New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island. New Brunswick would have been entitled to $7,517 and Prince Edward Island to $1,915. That would be the total amount to which they would be entitled out of $200,000, and they have not availed themselves of the grant.	.
The remaining provinces have taken the whole of the amounts to which they are entitled?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Yes, but unless quite
recently, they have not been paid the full amounts to which they are entitled. Generally speaking-I am speaking broadly, there may be one or two exceptions-all the provinces have expended far more than the grants paid to them. For example, I find that Manitoba has a grant from us of $6,305 and, according to the last figures available, she spent on this work $30,201.
Is that all that was allotted to Manitoba?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: , $12,611 would be the total grant for the year. I find that Saskatchewan was entitled to $15,361 and the last figure that we have available indicates that Saskatchewan, in dealing with the problem, spent $53,571. Thus most of the provinces are spending far in excess of the grants which they are paid.

They are earning the
subsidy all right?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Grant to assist the Canadian Association for the Prevention of Tuberculosis, $10,000.

Will the minister
explain this item?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
This is an old grant
which has been carried on from year to year. I think it was first started in the

year 1902 when it began with the grant of $1,000, and it was gradually increased to $5,000. In 1910, the amount became $10,000, and $10,000 has been paid annually since then. This Association was formed some years ago and it is still
11 p.m. being carried on under Dr.
Porter, who is the secretary. It has interested itself during all these years in the care and treatment of tuberculous patients. I think it may be said that, as a result of the activities of this organization, there has been established throughout Canada from coast to coast a series of sanatoria that have done a splendid work in caring for this class of patients. From my general knowledge of the situation I would say that their work is not yet through. It is now very largely of an educative nature, and I think it might very profitably continue for a while at any rate.
What can you do with $10,000? That is nothing.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I presume they get other funds as well.:

The association gets
very large subscriptions from the public. This grant has been made for a number of years, and I think very properly. I have been connected with the activities of the association all over Canada, and I think the grant is a very small one. The association is supported largely by the public, and their work is commended in all respects. Dr. Porter is the secretary. He travels a good deal and any one who has come in contact with him and heard his lectures will agree that they are very, very instructive and useful.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Grant towards defraying the expenses of the Canadian National Committee for Mental Hygiene, $10,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: This grant was first paid in the year 1919-20. This organization was formed for the purpose of investigating the mental condition of at least some of our people-those found in asylums and jails and other institutions of that character. Dr. Martin, of Montreal, is president, and the executive consists of Drs. Clarke, Mundie, and Hincks. I had the privilege two years ago of meeting a committee representing these gentlemen and discussing their work with them. I got a good many of their reports at that time, and went through them, and in my judgment the association is carrying on a very valuable work. They have assisted the provinces very materially. They have made a survey of the institutions in Ontario, Quebec and Manitoba, and I know they have had an invitation to do so in Saskatchewan, but I do not know whether they have yet visited that province. Their survey was undertaken mainly with the object in view of advising these provinces as to the treatment of mental defectives. I remember meeting one of the doctors from Quebec, Dr. Desloges, who is Superintendent of Health for that province. He was very pleased with the work this association had done in that province and with the assistance he had received. It is proposed that this grant should be continued this year. Whether or not it should be . continued after that, will be a matter to be decided in the future. I have no hesitation in saying that these gentlemen have done very valuable work. When the association started, they collected $50,000 by private subscription, and it was only after collecting that amount that they came to us because their Budget covered a very much larger sum. They came to us for a grant of some $10,000. I presume that within the last two years they have raised large amounts by private subscriptions. In any event, I think they are doing a very valuable work.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Progress reported.

speakerposition: subtopic
stagedirection
speechtext: House again in Committee on Bill 118, to amend the Bankruptcy Act, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: When this Bill was last before the committee, on Tuesday, May 3, all of its clauses had been read and considered; a majority of them had been adopted, but clauses 11, 12, 40, 41, 42 and 43 had been allowed to stand. Mr. Guthrie had also proposed to amend clause 11 by inserting after the word "Act" in line 51, on page 4 of the Bill, the following words: "for the purposes of such meeting," but this amendment had not been adopted.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: I think the amendment has now been practically agreed to.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Amendment agreed to.
Section 11, as amended, agreed to.
Section 12, agreed to.
On the motion of Mr. Guthrie the committee by unanimous consent returned to

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: the consideration of clause 8-receiving order or assignment to be filed:

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
I move to strike out clause 8 and substitute therefor the following :
The Act is amended by inserting immediately after section ten, the following:-
Every authorized trustee to whom an assignment is made under section nine of this Act Shad] within four days of such assignment fyle, in the Court having jurisdiction in the locality of the debtor, the said assignment, and should another authorized trustee be subsequently appointed in his stead such other trustee shall within four days of his appointment give notice thereof to the said court.
I am taking this clause from the Bill now before the House introduced by my hon. friend from George Etienne Cartier (Mr. Jacobs).
Section as amended agreed to.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
I move to insert, immediately after section 8, as section 8 (a) the following:
