Section 5 is amended by adding as sub-section (2) the following: (2) the said interim receiver may, under the direction of the court, summarily dispose of any perishable goods and carry on the business of the debtor for all conservatory purposes.
That clause is suggested by Mr. Justice Panneton, judge of the Superior Court of Quebec.
There is no definition of the word "conservatory" in the clause. Is it left to the judgment of the judge?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: It only applies to perishable goods.

I did not know the
word "perishable" was in the clause.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Section agreed to.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
I move to insert as
clause 8 (b) the following:
Paragraph (to) of sub-section 1 of section 11 is amended by adding at the end thereof the following words: "and except also the rights of a secured creditor under section six of this Act."
_ This is suggested by the same learned judge of the province of Quebec.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Section agreed to.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: I move to amend section 40 by replacing in lines 10 and 11, the word "one" by the word "three."
That is to say, under the new law the landlord will be entitled to six months' rent, three months past due, and three months accelerative?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Amendment agreed to.

Section as amended agreed to.
Sections 41, 42 and 43 agreed to.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
I move to add to the Bill, as clauses 52 and 53 thereof, the following:
52.	The French version of The Bankruptcy Act, chapter thirty-six of the statutes of 1919, is hereby amended by striking out the words "tenir maison" in the last line of paragraph (d) of section three thereof, and substitutisg therefor the words "se renfermer dans sa maison."
53.	Section eleven of the said French version of the said Act is further amended by striking out'the word "meubles" and replacing it by the word "rgels" in the eighteenth and twenty-third lines of subsection one, in the eighth line of subsection eight, in the fifth line of subsection nine and in the seventh line of subsection eleven.
Would the hon. member who suggested that amendment please explain it?

When I introduced the Bill originally, I explained that the French version is not quite in accordance with the law as it was intended to be placed on the statute book. The words "tenir maison" are in the statute instead of the words "se renfermer dans sa maison." That is, in the section itself one of the acts of bankruptcy which the insolvent can commit is "keeping house," and the party who translated the expression into French, instead of saying "se renfermer dans sa maison" translated it literally and said "tenir maison," which means that the insolvent keeps house or is a housekeeper, which is not an act of bankruptcy. The amendment is purely for the purpose of bringing both versions into harmony. [DOT]

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Sections agreed to.	.

Before the Bill is reported, I would draw to the attention of the Acting Solicitor General the question of the remuneration of the trustee and of the solicitor. Section 40 of the Act deals with the remuneration of the trustee, and another section, which I have not before me, provides for the remuneration of the solicitor of the estate. The law says that the trustee is entitled to a remuneration of 5 per cent. Section 3 of section 40 provides that the remuneration of the trustee shall not, under any circumstances, exceed 5 per cent of the cash receipts. Subsequently, when the general rules under the Bankruptcy Act were passed, a table of fees was provided, under which the trustee is entitled to various fees for different services which he renders while managing the estate. The trustees in bankruptcy in the province of Quebec,-I do not know

what they do in the other provinces-not only credit themselves with five per cent remuneration, but also with these fees, and in many cases the trustee walks off with the entire estate. Now this law was passed for the purpose of keeping down costs and seeing that the creditors get something out of the estate, but the creditors now find they are in a very much worse position than they were before this Act was passed. I should- like to know from the Acting Solicitor General whether it was intended that these trustees should receive the remuneration provided for in section 40 and also the fees referred to in the general rules? Whatever I have said also applies to the solicitor's themselves. If it is a fact that both the solicitors and the trustees are entitled to the five per cent each, plus these fees as provided under the general rules, we would like to know forthwith because, as I said before, the Act will not function very long if this is allowed to remain in force.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
I thought, Mr. Chairman, that the Act was very clear and definite upon the question of costs and the question of fees. The whole remuneration of the trustees is dealt with under section 40, and subsection 3 of section 40 is very specific. It says:
The remuneration of the trustee for all services shall not under any circumstances exceed five per cent of the cash receipts.
That is an absolute limitation, and that is for all the services that he performs. But in any event his fees are again limited to such an amount as the creditors shall see fit to vote to him. He is not entitled to exceed that limit or to collect another bill of costs or fees as provided by the tariff contained in the general rules. I think the tariff in the general rules was provided for the purpose of fixing the fees of solicitors and attorneys, but in any case the fees of solicitors and attorneys shall not exceed the amount specified in section 67 of the Act.	.
Not even with the consent of the creditors?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
No, the debtor would be the sufferer then. Section 67 is pretty definite. It provides:
All attorneys, solicitors and counsel acting for the trustee or for the estate of a debtor in respect of proceedings under this Act, shall be paid out of the assets of such estate their reasonable costs and fees as fixed in a tariff provided by General Rules ;-
We have the tariff. It goes on to say:
but, except as hereinafter provided, the aggregate amount of such oosts and fees so payable out of the assets of estates whereof the gross proceeds exceed five thousand dollars shall not exceed five "per centum of such gross proceeds.
That is in estates over five thousand. Then as to smaller estates there is this provision:	[DOT]
This provision shall not disentitle such attorneys, solicitors and counsel to any costs or fees which may be awarded against or be payable by persons other than the trustee or the estate of the debtor, and notwithstanding anything in this Act- contained, in estates whereof the gross proceeds do not exceed five thousand dollars, the costs or fees payable may, by unanimous vote of the inspectors, be increased to any amount not to exceed ten per centum of the gross proceeds of such estate. Such tariff shall direct by whom and in what manner such costs and fees are to be collected and accounted for and to what account they shall be paid.
I think it is quite clear under that section that in estates where the amount realized is over $5,000, solicitors or attorneys shall be paid according to the tariff, but the whole of their costs shall not exceed five per centum. In smaller estates under $5,000, if the inspectors of the estate unanimously agree, then these fees may be up to ten per cent of the amount of the estate, but they are not entitled to their commission and also their bill of costs. I have been told that in some parts of Canada a practice has grown up that a solicitor gets his commission and likewise a bill of costs. All I can say is it is contrary to the spirit and letter of the law and such a custom should not be allowed to prevail.

Has the Secretary of
State any disciplinary power over the trustee and solicitor?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
He is deliberately
breaking the law.

I invite my hon. friend's attention to page 83 of the rules of practice, the general rules, in which an elaborate system of counsel fees is published. I see that they run up from $10 in some cases to $50 in others. Then in section 88, on page 84 I find this:
Solicitors fees on collection of account claims, collected after notice on demand and owing as a whole or in instalments, on the first $300 or less, fifteen per cent; on the excess over $300 up to $1,000, eight per cent; on over $1,000, four per cent; Minimum charge $5.
Is that also included in the five per cent which the solicitor is entitled to receive?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
I understand that
everything collected, no matter what the bill of costs is, must not exceed the percentage set out in scetion 67 of. the Act. Now I realize that these rules do not in

all respects conform to what I consider to be the meaning of the Act, and I think the rules, in the near future, will have to he re-drafted. There are a number of inconsistencies between the rules and various sections of the Act. I think when they are re-drafted care should be taken to lay down expressly in the rules that the solicitors or attorneys shall not in any case accept more than the percentages set out in 67.

Before the section is
settled, may I point out that nothing is said about disbursements, and I can imagine a case where the disbursements in a small estate might, for some unaccountable reason, run high.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: There is a provision for the disbursements of a trustee in another section af the Act.

Would it not be a good
idea for the Secretary of State to circularize the trustees who have been appointed, and of whom he has a list, drawing their attention to the fact that in some cases the law is being contravened, and that they must adhere strictly to the letter of the law in the future.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Yes, I think something of the kind should be done.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Title agreed to.
Bill^ reported, and amendments read a second time and concurred in.
On the motion of Right Hon. Mr. Meighen the House adjourned at 11.35 p.m.
Tuesday, May 10, 1921.
